Scientists discover a plastic-eating âPac-Manâ enzyme with a surprising secret

- Scientists have discovered a remarkable âPac-Man enzymeâ that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

Plastic pollution is one of the world's most persistent environmental problems. Vast amounts of discarded plastic accumulate in the oceans, sometimes forming enormous garbage patches that threaten marine life. Most conventional plastics break down extremely slowly because microorganisms struggle to digest the synthetic polymers from which they are made. Instead of disappearing, these materials gradually fragment into increasingly smaller particles, including microplastics and nanoplastics.

Yet plastic waste is not completely beyond the reach of nature. Bacteria and other microorganisms can colonize its surfaces, forming communities known as biofilms. These communities create a distinctive microbial ecosystem that scientists call the "plastisphere."

Researchers at the University of Konstanz have now discovered an unusual enzyme that could reveal how some bacteria are becoming better equipped to break down certain types of plastic. The enzyme can digest particular polyesters and biodegradable plastics, but it has another unexpected ability: it can also break down penicillin, suggesting a possible connection to antibiotic resistance.

Scientists have nicknamed it the "Pac-Man enzyme" because its molecular structure features a remarkably wide opening where chemical reactions take place, known as the active site. The discovery suggests that bacteria may be adapting to digest certain plastic materials more quickly than researchers previously believed.

However, the findings also highlight an important limitation. For microorganisms to make a meaningful difference in reducing plastic pollution, more plastic products would need to be made from biodegradable materials that contain chemical bonds microbes can break apart.
Testing How Bacteria Break Down Bioplastics

To investigate how microorganisms digest biodegradable plastics, University of Konstanz biologists Harry Lerner and David Schleheck studied the entire process of microbial decomposition. They wanted to determine not only whether the materials could be completely broken down, but also which microorganisms were responsible and what biological mechanisms allowed them to do it.

The researchers examined the composition of the microbial communities involved and analyzed their collective genetic information (the metagenome). This approach allowed them to search for genes that might produce enzymes capable of breaking apart plastic polymers.

Their experiments focused on long-chain aliphatic polyesters (LCAP), a class of biodegradable plastic materials developed by a research team led by chemist Stefan Mecking. These materials contain chemical bonds that certain microorganisms can potentially break down, unlike the more resistant structures found in many conventional plastics.
The collaborative findings were published in The ISME Journal.
To observe how the bioplastics behaved in a natural environment, the team placed samples beneath the surface of forest soil at the university's botanical garden.
"We buried small pieces of LCAP bioplastic film in the upper humus layer in the forest at the university's botanical garden, about ten centimeters deep," explains Harry Lerner.
"This layer is where the breakdown of cellulose and other natural polymers, such as cutin - a plant-based polyester - takes place."

Humus is the upper layer of soil rich in decomposing organic matter, where microorganisms play a major role in recycling nutrients. Cellulose is the main structural component of plant cell walls, while cutin is a naturally occurring polyester that helps form the protective outer covering of plants.
The researchers selected this environment because its microorganisms already possess the biological machinery needed to break down complex natural materials.
Bioplastics Disappeared Within About a Year

Alongside the outdoor experiment, the scientists carried out laboratory tests using soil collected from the same forest. They mixed powdered bioplastics into the soil and monitored microbial activity over the course of an entire year.

One important measurement was the amount of carbon dioxide, or CO2, released from the samples. As microorganisms consume and metabolize organic materials, they produce carbon dioxide through respiration. Tracking this gas helped the researchers determine how actively the microbes were breaking down the plastics.
The buried plastic films remained in the forest soil for a full year, allowing the team to compare decomposition under natural conditions with the carefully monitored laboratory experiments.
To assess the results, the scientists also tested cellulose, other biodegradable plastics, conventional polyethylene plastic, and soil samples without added materials.

"Cellulose, other types of bioplastics such as PHBV and PCL, as well as high-density plastic (HDPE) and untreated soil were used as controls in the laboratory. We found that all bioplastic materials were completely degraded within roughly 250 to 330 days. Cellulose broke down after about 80 days, whereas virtually no degradation occurred for HDPE," says Lerner.

The difference was striking. While the biodegradable plastics were completely broken down within approximately nine to eleven months, conventional high-density polyethylene showed almost no decomposition.

These results demonstrate why the chemical makeup of plastic matters so much. Some polymers contain bonds that microbial enzymes can attack, allowing bacteria to dismantle them into smaller molecules. Others, including widely used polyethylene, are far more resistant to biological degradation.
Mysterious Holes Reveal How Bacteria Eat Plastic
When the researchers recovered the plastic films from the forest soil, they discovered something unexpected.

Using electron microscopy, which can reveal structures far too small to see with an ordinary light microscope, the team examined the surfaces of the buried materials. They found numerous tiny holes, each approximately matching the dimensions and shape of an individual bacterial cell.
The unusual pattern suggested that bacteria were doing more than simply attaching themselves to the plastic. They appeared to be breaking into the material itself.

"We hypothesized that bacteria are coated with plastic-depolymerases anchored to their cell surfaces. This would enable them to digest their way into the material and become embedded within the film, leaving behind microscopic holes of exactly this type," explains Lerner.

Depolymerases are enzymes that break large molecules called polymers into smaller chemical units. If these enzymes are attached directly to the outside of a bacterium, they could allow the microorganism to digest the surrounding material while remaining in close contact with it.

This would help explain the microscopic cavities observed in the plastic films. Rather than relying entirely on enzymes released into the environment, the bacteria might be able to break down the material directly at their surfaces.
Scientists Identify the Plastic-Eating "Pac-Man Enzyme"
To find the biological machinery behind this unusual behavior, Lerner extracted DNA from the entire community of microorganisms living in the soil samples.
He then sequenced the genetic material and carefully analyzed the extensive data to determine which microbes and genes became especially abundant as the bioplastics decomposed.
One gene stood out. It was strongly enriched specifically in forest soil containing LCAP, suggesting that it could play an important role in breaking down the biodegradable polyester.

Further analysis revealed that the gene produces an esterase, a type of enzyme capable of splitting certain chemical bonds found in esters. These bonds are present in many naturally occurring substances as well as in various biodegradable polyesters.
What made this particular enzyme especially interesting was how it was positioned on bacterial cells.
Its genetic instructions included a secretion signal that directs the enzyme outside the cell, along with a lipid anchor that holds it firmly to the cell membrane.

This arrangement means the enzyme can remain attached to the bacterium's surface while attacking nearby plastic molecules. Its unusually exposed active site also provides space for the enzyme to interact with polymer chains.
The researchers had identified the molecular mechanism they were looking for, along with the enzyme they named "Pac-Man."
A Surprising Connection to Antibiotic Resistance
The discovery became even more intriguing when scientists examined the enzyme's molecular structure.
Although it resembled esterases, which are known for breaking down ester bonds, it also shared structural similarities with another important family of bacterial enzymes: beta-lactamases.

These enzymes are well known for their role in antibiotic resistance. Some bacteria produce beta-lactamases that disable antibiotics such as penicillin by breaking open a critical part of their chemical structure, known as the beta-lactam ring.

"Its structure resembles that of esterases, but also that of beta-lactamases, which are bacterial enzymes that are capable of cleaving the beta-lactam ring of certain antibiotics, such as penicillin, thereby making bacteria resistant to antibiotics," says Lerner.
Laboratory experiments confirmed that the newly discovered enzyme was capable of performing both types of chemical reactions.
It could break polyester chains into their individual building blocks, known as monomers, while also cleaving penicillin.
This dual activity was particularly surprising because plastic degradation and antibiotic breakdown are usually considered separate biological functions.

The finding raises the possibility that some enzymes involved in plastic decomposition could also contribute to antibiotic resistance. However, demonstrating that an enzyme can chemically break down penicillin in the laboratory does not establish that it provides antibiotic resistance to living bacteria.
Could Plastic-Eating Bacteria Help Solve Plastic Pollution?
The discovery also raises a broader question about how rapidly microorganisms can adapt to synthetic materials introduced into their environment.
For most of Earth's history, plastic pollution did not exist. Microorganisms evolved enzymes to digest naturally occurring substances, including plant fibers and other complex organic molecules.
Modern plastics have introduced an enormous new collection of potential carbon sources into the environment, but many of these materials remain chemically inaccessible to microbes.
"The plastisphere is a new habitat in our environment," explains Schleheck.

"Humans have only been introducing plastic into the environment in significant quantities for around 50 to 75 years. Since then, it has theoretically been available to microbial communities - such as bacteria, yeasts and fungi - as an additional source of carbon and energy for their growth. By 'theoretically', I mean that they would certainly like to use the plastic as a growth substrate - but they cannot, because the materials are actually indigestible to microbial metabolism and are therefore hardly degraded."
The Pac-Man enzyme suggests that this barrier may not be absolute for every type of plastic.
Some bacteria appear capable of using specialized enzymes to attack biodegradable polyesters, potentially allowing them to exploit these materials as sources of energy and nutrients.

For scientists studying plastic pollution, the finding offers a promising clue about how biological degradation might be improved. It also suggests that microbial communities could be adapting to certain synthetic polymers more rapidly than previously anticipated.

However, the results do not mean that bacteria are suddenly capable of consuming the enormous amounts of conventional plastic already accumulating in the environment. The experiments showed that polyethylene remained largely unaffected, even as the biodegradable plastics decomposed.
Instead, the researchers emphasize the importance of designing materials that microorganisms can actually digest.

"I find this encouraging, because it seems that bacteria can adapt to breaking down polyester plastics more quickly than we expected. To tackle the environmental problem of plastic pollution, we humans need to work with the capabilities of microbes. Ideally, this would involve using only polymers with biochemical breaking points, such as the hydrolysable ester bonds in polyesters like LCAP or other types of bioplastics," concludes Schleheck.

The discovery offers a glimpse of a potentially more sustainable approach to plastic production. Rather than expecting microorganisms to break down materials that are naturally resistant to decomposition, scientists could develop plastics with chemical structures that make biological recycling possible.

The Pac-Man enzyme illustrates how bacteria can exploit these molecular weak points, offering new insight into the relationship between plastic pollution, microbial adaptation, and the future of biodegradable materials.

NASA captures strange waves high above Hurricane Simon

- As Hurricane Simon unleashed destructive winds and flooding along Mexicoâs coast, NASA satellites captured an extraordinary sight: massive atmospheric waves rippling high above the storm. The rare images reveal how powerful hurricanes can disturb the upper atmosphere, creating patterns that are usually invisible from space.

Despite remaining offshore, Hurricane Simon battered Mexico's Pacific coast with powerful winds and flooding. At the same time, NASA satellites captured an extraordinary sight high above the storm: enormous waves rippling through Earth's upper atmosphere.

Hurricane Simon was the latest in a series of powerful tropical cyclones to sweep across the Eastern Pacific during the 2026 hurricane season. On October 11, 2026, the Category 4 hurricane moved dangerously close to Mexico's coastline as it traveled north-northwest, with sustained winds reaching 250 kilometers (155 miles) per hour.
Hurricane Simon Batters Mexico's Pacific Coast

At approximately 2:30 p.m. local time (20:30 Universal Time) on October 11, the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) instrument aboard NASA's Suomi NPP satellite captured an image of the massive storm. At that moment, Simon's eye was located roughly 50 kilometers (30 miles) offshore, between the coastal cities of Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta.

According to the National Hurricane Center (NHC), sustained winds had weakened to approximately 210 kilometers (130 miles) per hour by the time the image was taken. However, the hurricane's powerful inner core was still moving close enough to threaten communities along the coast.

The Sierra Madre mountains appeared to help limit Simon's strength, with the rugged terrain reducing the storm's intensity and shrinking the area affected by its winds. Even so, the hurricane brought torrential rainfall and flooding to coastal communities, including the port city of Manzanillo. The heavy rain also increased the threat of dangerous mudslides in mountainous regions, according to news reports.
NASA Captures Strange Waves Above the Hurricane
While Simon churned across the Pacific, satellites detected something remarkable happening far above the clouds.

During the early morning of October 11, the storm generated rippling disturbances that traveled into Earth's upper atmosphere. A nighttime satellite image, captured by the VIIRS instrument aboard NOAA-21, revealed atmospheric gravity waves spreading outward from the hurricane.

These waves are created by intense activity within the storm. Near the hurricane's eyewall, the release of latent heat fuels powerful convection, causing warm, moist air to surge upward and form towering cumulonimbus clouds.

The strong updrafts inside these clouds can disturb the surrounding atmosphere, generating waves that travel upward into the stratosphere and mesosphere. Unlike ocean waves, which move through water, atmospheric gravity waves are disturbances that propagate through the air, with gravity acting as a restoring force.
Why the Rare Atmospheric Ripples Were Visible

Although powerful hurricanes can generate atmospheric gravity waves, satellites cannot always detect them. Strong winds at high altitudes can weaken or disperse the disturbances before they reach the mesosphere, where they may become visible through a phenomenon known as airglow.

Airglow is a faint, natural light produced by gases high in Earth's atmosphere. When atmospheric gravity waves pass through this glowing region, they create subtle variations in brightness that can reveal their distinctive ripple patterns.

The VIIRS instrument's day-night band is sensitive enough to detect this faint light. However, it also captures moonlight reflected from Earth's surface and atmosphere, which can make the much weaker airglow difficult to distinguish.

Fortunately, conditions were unusually favorable when the satellite observed Simon. With very little illumination from the Moon, the delicate atmospheric ripples stood out more clearly, allowing the satellite to capture the striking patterns.
Hurricane Simon's Unpredictable Path Raises Concerns
By the morning of October 13, meteorologists were still struggling to predict where Simon would go next and how strong it might become.
The National Hurricane Center described confidence in its intensity and track forecasts as "very low confidence," reflecting how the storm had repeatedly behaved differently than expected.
At the time, one possibility was that Simon could turn northward, enter the Gulf of California, and eventually make landfall.

Regardless of its exact path, large ocean swells generated by the hurricane were expected to create hazardous conditions along portions of Mexico's southwestern and west-central coastlines in the following days.

In the annals of 'cat parasite' research, Toxoplasma gondii grabs most of the headlines.

The mysterious pathogen, which may infect up to one-third of the global population, is famous for altering the behavior of its hosts, and it's also of serious concern for its varying effects on human health.
But T. gondii isn't the only parasite that cats and humans have the misfortune of sharing.

In a new study published in PLOS One, scientists shine a spotlight on a protozoan pest called Giardia duodenalis, and the research team says it's the largest investigation to date on the parasite's prevalence in domestic cats in North America.

While most infections with G. duodenalis don't produce symptoms, it can result in the disease giardiasis in both humans and animals, which can cause diarrhea, abdominal pain, weakness, and other signs of poor health, including failure to grow in animals.

In the study, led by veterinarian and first author Margaret Wingerd from VCA SouthPaws Veterinary Specialists & Emergency Center in Fairfax, Virginia, researchers analyzed more than 157,000 stool samples collected from domestic cats across the US and Canada.
Using PCR testing, the team identified G. duodenalis in 9,962 of the samples analyzed, corresponding to an overall detection rate of 6.3 percent – approximately one in every 16 cats tested.
Of those positive samples, 1,840 (18.5 percent) were detections of the A or B assemblages of the parasite with zoonotic potential, which means the infection could potentially spread to humans.
Among cats that carried the parasite, a number of patterns were identified.
Generally, male cats were slightly more likely to be infected than female cats, and younger cats were more likely to be infected than older cats.

Kittens showed a much higher rate of positive cases (10.7 percent) compared to senior cats of 10 years or older (1.3 percent), and kittens also showed the highest proportion of assemblage A/B positivity (19.9 percent).
Adult cats that had not been spayed or neutered were generally more likely to carry the parasite than their sterilized counterparts, although the opposite pattern was observed in kittens.

The researchers speculate that the higher odds in males and intact cats may be due to exposure differences because of housing differences (indoor versus outdoor), increased roaming behavior, or differences in immune competency.

With regard to kittens showing greater chances of infection than older cats, the researchers say it could reflect greater acquired immunity in older animals, or may also indicate differences in exposure due to housing and activity.

In terms of geography, cats in the US Midwest had the highest overall detection rate (7.8 percent), while cats in the Northeast had the highest proportion of potentially zoonotic variants among positive samples (21.6 percent).
Seasonal differences also seem to matter, with significantly lower detection rates in summer (4.6 percent) compared to winter (8.1 percent).
"G. duodenalis cysts can survive for a prolonged time in cool and moist environments," the researchers write.
"This could explain the lower infection rate in summer in general, as summer tends to be warm and dry, and cysts are less likely to survive."
All told, the findings show that only about 1.2 percent of the more than 157,000 samples tested carried parasites that could potentially infect people.
While this represents a relatively small proportion of the cats tested, the researchers say the prevalence of the parasite warrants caution and careful monitoring.
"Given the ability of G. duodenalis to infect a wide variety of hosts including people and animals, this protozoan can present a public health concern," the study authors write.

"Based on our results, about 18 percent of cats in the US and Canada infected with G. duodenalis have potential zoonotic assemblages. This highlights the need for routine fecal screening in domestic cats, especially in cats at a higher risk for G. duodenalis or those living in households with young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised people."
In the twilight deeps of the Eastern Pacific Ocean, a magical sight can be found on a seamount off the coast of Costa Rica.

As the underwater vehicle SuBastian glides over a rocky outcrop oddly coated with a fuzzy pink patina and punctuated with basket-shaped gleaming white sponges, a majestic yellow form emerges from the darkness.
It looks like a golden tree, so vividly yellow you can imagine it glowing.
Then, as the camera zooms closer, you can see the pink fuzz moving – a thick carpet of stars from which the golden tree blooms.
The stars, of course, are not real stars, but a teeming multitude of pink brittle stars; nor is the golden tree a real tree.
Instead, it's a species of octocoral unlike any scientists have ever seen – one so unusual that it required a whole new branch of the tree of life to accommodate its strangeness.

In a paper describing the species, researchers led by Odalisca Breedy of the University of Costa Rica have named the coral Laurinque elenya – a name derived from Tolkien's Elvish language Quenya, meaning "golden tree of the stars".
You can see the golden coral forest for yourself in the footage from SuBastian's dive, starting at around the 20-minute mark in the video below.
Corals – for all the resemblance many of them bear to plants – are animals, and they take many different forms adapted to life beneath the waves.
Octocorals are one specific group containing more than 3,000 species, named for the eightfold symmetry of the tiny polyps that line their branches.

They are a diverse bunch, and their number includes some very strange colonies indeed – so when Laurinque was found at depths of 360 to 529 meters (1,181 to 1,735 feet) during dives in 2019 and 2023, it would not have surprised scientists to find it had a few idiosyncrasies.
But Laurinque wasn't just another eccentric aunt in a family full of them.
Its colonies can grow more than a meter tall and 1.2 meters wide, with densely branching structures covered in unusually elongated polyps – the tiny animals that collectively make up a coral colony.
These polyps can partially retract into the branches, and the microscopic skeletal structures that support the coral, called sclerites, have a distinctive assortment of shapes.
Together, these features – found in different octocoral groups, but not together in a single species in this way – made it difficult to match Laurinque with any known family of octocorals.
And its DNA only exacerbated the conundrum.

The researchers analyzed three genetic markers from the coral's DNA, comparing them with sequences from other octocorals to see where their mysterious specimen belonged on the evolutionary family tree.
They got a match on a mitochondrial gene.
Then they got another one on the other mitochondrial gene.
Normally, this would be good news – a slam dunk that could confidently place a vexing species into a clean category.
Unfortunately, both markers matched with different octocoral families. One placed it strongly in Incrustatidae. The other was equally strong for placement in Eunicellidae.
And they couldn't even use the third marker – ribosomal DNA – as a tiebreaker. It was magnificently inconclusive.

So, after several years of not knowing, they had to bring out the big guns – the collection of new specimens, followed by an analysis of hundreds of genetic regions from Laurinque. And that, finally, yielded an answer.
The coral, Breedy and her colleagues found, is closely related to Eunicellidae – but still distinct from it, the first known member of the Laurinqueidae coral family.

"I saw the octocoral garden for the first time in 2019, and I was impressed by the beauty of the landscape, which inspired, later the elvish name of the taxa. I thought the species could belong to a known family and genera, but after the preliminary morphological analysis I realized that it was something very different that I could not match with the known taxa," Breedy said.

"In 2023 we collected more samples and thanks to the exhaustive molecular analyses made by my colleagues, Cathy McFadden, Catalina Murillo and Andrea Quattrini, we were able to determine the taxonomic placement of the stunning species, in one of the most enigmatic sites."
But there's more than a whole new coral family to the discovery.
The golden coral gardens grow in waters with extremely low oxygen levels, at temperatures between 8 and 11 degrees Celsius (46 and 52 degrees Fahrenheit).
These conditions would be inhospitable to many animals, yet Laurinque forms elaborate, ethereal underwater forests, its branches rising above a seafloor almost completely obscured by brittle stars.

Such coral gardens are important habitats in the deep ocean. Their intricate, three-dimensional structures provide places for other animals to shelter, feed, and thrive, helping support biodiversity in a deeply challenging environment.
And Laurinque may not be confined to Costa Rica. The researchers report possible sightings off Panama and the Galápagos Islands, although these have yet to be confirmed.

For now, the golden tree of the stars remains a poignant and magical reminder of how much of Earth's biodiversity is still waiting to be discovered – even in places where life seems almost impossible.
The research has been published in ZooKeys.

Around a decade ago Theranos, one of the buzziest science start-ups ever, imploded. Swamped by allegations of fraud, the actions of the company and its enigmatic CEO, Elizabeth Holmes, shone a harsh light on problems with scientific start-ups. Now scientists say these issues have only gotten worse.
In a new documentary titled You Can See Everything, filmmaker Nathan Fielder follows Holmes in the lead-up to starting a prison sentence in May 2023, after she was found guilty of fraud.

The film retraces the saga of Theranos, which claimed to have a machine that could perform hundreds of clinical tests using a single drop of blood. After years of fundraising, high-publicity support and partnerships with pharmacies to make the tests accessible, scientists and journalists revealed in 2015 that Theranos’s claims were false: there was no scientific evidence that its product worked.

Theranos is, in many ways, a cautionary tale and a relic of 2010s Silicon Valley. But for scientists, Theranos’s problems are anything but history.

John Ioannidis is a professor at Stanford University’s medical school and was among the first to question Theranos’s bona fides in a 2015 article. Eleven years later Ioannidis says he worries the problems of transparency and a lack of strong evidence in science and technology start-ups are, if anything, worse today.
“I feel kind of uneasy about this being presented as a sensationalist, movie-quality story [about] a single bad apple because I see very similar phenotypes to Theranos,” Ioannidis says.

Ioannidis argues that, in some ways, claims of scientific progress are a public relations game. As private companies have become increasingly powerful agents in driving research forward, the trend has shifted fields away from more traditional, publicly funded research and academia.
“Holmes is in jail, but the recipe of her success has been even more widely adopted,” he says.

Ian Papautsky, a microfluidics researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago, says that Theranos’s public downfall and time in the spotlight create a strong case for validating scientific findings. But he, too, worries that, as start-ups and private companies increasingly drive discovery, opportunities for secrecy or fraud may grow.

“Many of the start-ups are not transparent in their technology development,” he says. “On the one hand, you would argue that they have to be, because they’re trying to compete with everyone else. But that also makes it a lot easier to hide the mismanagement and all these other various issues.”

Holmes’s husband, Billy Evans, who also appears in the documentary, is himself quietly building a new blood testing company. The start-up, called Haemanthus, plans to use artificial intelligence tools to run diagnostic tests. Holmes is listed as a scientific adviser to the company, and Evans has raised millions of dollars in funding, according to NPR.
“The idea is to put the band back together and do it all again,” Evans tells Fielder in the movie.

Theranos has made it harder for academics who study blood testing or microfluidics to get funding, says Umut Gurkan, a biotechnology researcher at Case Western Reserve University. He creates blood testing products for conditions such as sickle cell anemia. Gurkan remembers going to Silicon Valley in 2015 to seek funding and being told, “We don’t invest in diagnostics anymore.”
Even as diagnostic technology has advanced, it remains difficult to bring it into markets, he says.

“Trust in science is fragile, and ‘a drop of blood’ now sounds like a scam,” Gurkan says. “Honest companies trying to save lives pay that tax. And at the end of the day, patients and real people pay the price with lack of working diagnostics and technologies that deserve to be in the market.”

As for Theranos’s claims: even after more than 10 years of advancement in clinical testing and microfluidics, its premise remains impossible, the researchers consulted for this article say—at least at the scale that Holmes promised. A drop of blood doesn’t hold nearly enough biological information to conduct the hundreds of tests that Theranos claimed.
Theranos’s mission was noble, Papautsky says, but the science did not and does not hold up.

“Doing multiplex testing on a small volume of blood is a good concept—it would be an important advancement in technology,” he says. “But having experts with the right knowledge and good management is very important, and it’s becoming more and more important these days. Expertise is not necessarily being valued as it used to be.”

The beginning of fall and back-to-school time means cold virus season has arrived. Usually, colds hit as lesser-evil infections before influenza season takes over. But already, the flu is popping up early in pockets of the U.S. Here’s why that might be and everything else you need to know as we head into the dreaded annual flu season.

According to the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention’s latest FluView report, released on October 9, flu activity has been climbing since early September. Flu season in the U.S. generally begins gaining momentum in the fall, with activity peaking between December and February. But surveillance indicators show that certain strains of influenza are rising fast. The CDC’s latest data show a nationwide percent positivity rate for influenza—the percentage of all positive influenza tests—of 3.6 percent. That’s a sixfold increase compared with this time in 2025, when the rate was 0.6 percent.

Parts of the U.S. are showing much higher positive rates. The CDC splits the country up into regions, and Region 9, which includes Arizona, California, Hawaii and Nevada, had 9.5 percent positivity, according to the latest data. Experts say that is exceptionally high for this time of year.

“It’s not unheard of to see things rising at this stage,” says Andrew Pekosz, an immunologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “But it’s also something that we probably shouldn’t be seeing until maybe November or December at the earliest.”

Flu can be caused by different types of influenza, including influenza A (and its subtypes) and influenza B. Usually, flu season brings a mix of types. Right now, in the areas of the country with the highest positivity rates, H1N1, a subtype of influenza A, is dominant. According to the CDC, the most recent weekly testing data showed that 98.4 percent of the positive tests indicated H1N1 and that 1.6 percent revealed H3N2, another influenza A subtype.
Still, experts say it’s too early to predict whether these spikes could signal a particularly severe winter flu season.
Will this year’s flu vaccines work well?

One of the best ways to protect yourself from the flu is to get a flu vaccine. Every year experts reformulate these vaccines depending on what strains of the virus are circulating or predicted to circulate during the coming winter season.

Whichever subtype dominates matters because it can help predict which groups will experience the greatest disease burden. It can also determine how well existing immunity will protect people, as well as how the year’s flu vaccines will perform.

H1N1 and H3N2 are both influenza A subtypes, but they are evolutionarily distinct and can affect people differently. H3N2-dominant seasons have historically been associated with particularly severe illness among older adults. H1N1, on the other hand, has had a greater effect on younger populations—but both can cause serious disease at any age.

“The version [of H1N1] that’s circulating seems to be a little bit different from the vaccine strain that we have and from H1N1 strains that have circulated before. It’s what we call an antigenic drift,” Pekosz says. That could be why the virus is emerging so early, he adds. If it can evade prior immunity, the pathogen will be easier to transmit.
But it’s still too early to know how that might influence the effectiveness of the current flu vaccines.
When is the best time to get vaccinated?
Trish Perl, a professor of internal medicine and a specialist in infectious disease at UT Southwestern Medical Center, says that right now is the best time to get a flu shot.

“Immunity from the flu vaccine is strongest for about four to six months, and we usually expect flu to peak in December or January,” Pekosz says. “So a September or October vaccination will get you through the worst part of the flu season.”

Perl agrees—she says that she often tells her people to, at the very least, get a flu vaccine before Thanksgiving. Because after that, she says, people have unlimited excuses for why they can’t find the time.
And with certain areas already seeing spikes, getting the shot earlier than usual may be best, Pekosz adds.
“The best time to get vaccinated is before you see influenza in your area,” he says.
What about the newly approved mRNA vaccine for flu?

On August 5, 2026, the Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna’s mFLUSIVA, the first mRNA seasonal influenza vaccine, for adults aged 50 and older. In a phase 3 clinical trial, the vaccine was found to be 26.6 percent more effective at preventing the flu than a standard flu shot.

FDA approval and inclusion in federal vaccination recommendations—informed by guidance by the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)—are separate regulatory steps, however. The disruption to ACIP under the Trump administration has made incorporating newly approved vaccines into guidance more complicated.
Moderna had said the vaccine would be available at select retailers during the 2026–2027 flu season. But so far, access appears to be limited.

Experts, including Pekosz and Perl, say that if people who qualify for the new mRNA vaccine have access to it, they should consider it. “The data would suggest that if you can get the mRNA vaccine, you probably will get a stronger response to most of the components in the vaccine than if you get the standard one. But again, the standard one is pretty good as well,” Pekosz says.

He and Perl are optimistic about the potential of mRNA technology to improve flu vaccines in the future. Because mRNA vaccines can be developed and manufactured more quickly than traditional shots, scientists could wait until later in the year before selecting which influenza strains to target. That added time could help us better predict which strains will circulate during flu season—ultimately meaning more effective vaccines.

The best thing anyone can do right now is to get their flu shot as soon as possible. And if you do end up getting sick, Perl says not to forget about antivirals, such as Tamiflu, which can be very effective and, in many cases, could reduce the amount of time you are infectious.

When a bee wants to tell its hive mates how to find a scrumptious field of flowers, it wiggles its rear end. A complicated combination of figure eight–like movements known as a waggle dance tells nearby bees what direction to fly in and how far to go. But what happens if a waggling bee is unsure of its directions?

A study published in Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology earlier this year shows that bees amplify their communication based on how certain they are that their information is true. It seems the more confident a bee is in what it’s conveying, the more emphatically it communicates with the hive, says study lead author Karmi Oxman, a behavioral ecologist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

“Confidence is sort of a human-y word, but it’s useful in this context,” Oxman says. Confidence reflects the communicator’s belief in a message’s relevance or reliability, “and the dance is a self-report of the situation in the field.” This extra information also prevents the bee from accidentally misleading the hive.

The experiment started with one bee flying to a specialized feeder. This first bee, also known as the focal bee, was always met with a sugar solution. The researchers then manipulated the scenario by changing what happened after the focal bee returned to the hive and gave directions to the feeder. In the “honest” scenario, the feeder remained full, and all the bees following the directions got a sugary treat. In the “liar” scenario, the feeder was found empty. And in the “unverified” scenario, all the bees were caught before they could return to the hive and report what happened.

When given the chance to communicate the feeder’s location to the hive again in a later experimental stage, the focal bee in the honest scenario tried harder to convince its fellows to visit the sugar source by performing more waggle dance circuits—suggesting the bee could assess the reliability of its own signal. Unverified and “liar” bees did not show that same increase; in fact, unverified bees decreased their recruitment efforts.

“For me, the big takeaway is that bees are not little robots,” says James C. Nieh, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, who was not involved in the study. “They’re getting information from their environment, and that [information] also includes how successful they are in communicating to their nest mates.”

Both Oxman and Nieh say they wonder what other types of communication beyond what we can see—such as chemical signals or vibrations—could be playing a role in waggle dances. Further research into how bees communicate can help with efforts to “maintain the world in a way that they can still thrive,” Nieh says.
Apple's iPhone Duo, its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January.
The company said in a statement that the preorder demand was "nothing short of extraordinary."
"We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said.

Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max.
The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol.

But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable.

Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units.
That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity.
"Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand.

Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem.

Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent Time profile.
"It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said.
The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated.
Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500.
Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share."
Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year.
That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity.
Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak told CNBC the firm expects initial demand to exceed supply.

Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available in the near term.
IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards.
"Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said.
And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before.

When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered the 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs.

That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products.
The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business.
IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026.

Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei.
According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025.
But the more important number for Apple may not be units.

A large share of Duo customers are expected to be existing iPhone owners, analysts said, including consumers who otherwise might have purchased a Pro Max and are now trading up to a device costing hundreds of dollars more.
Others could add the Duo as a second smartphone, with Apple's ecosystem allowing users to move relatively seamlessly between it and their primary iPhone.

Popal said that migration from roughly $1,200 premium iPhones to a device starting at nearly $2,000 should provide a "healthy boost" to Apple's revenue even if overall volumes remain relatively small.

The bank expects the Duo to have a disproportionate impact on iPhone revenue because of its much higher average selling price, even as overall iPhone shipments are expected to remain roughly flat next year.
JPMorgan said the iPhone 18 cycle is increasingly likely to be driven by price and product mix rather than unit growth.
D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said Apple needs the Duo to succeed as it comes up against a difficult set of earnings comps with its strongest upgrade cycle in years.
"Without an uplift from Duo, they may experience some pretty pedestrian revenue growth," Luria told CNBC.
The device gives Apple several ways to generate that uplift, he added.

It raises the company's average selling price by capturing die-hard Apple customers who might otherwise have bought a Pro Max. It could bring in some consumers who previously bought folding Android phones because Apple did not offer one. And it could create a halo around the rest of the iPhone lineup.
Luria said some consumers will visit Apple stores specifically to see the Duo, "but probably walk out with an iPhone or iPhone Pro at half the price."
That means the Duo can potentially help Apple even when someone decides not to buy it.
Lead times for the iPhone 18 Pro have softened in several markets compared with the prior cycle, while the more expensive Pro Max has held up better, according to JPMorgan's tracking.

Morgan Stanley has separately said its supply-chain checks are consistent with unusually early component order reductions for the Pro and Pro Max, though the firm has not yet seen evidence that those adjustments have translated into cuts to finished iPhone production.
That puts more pressure on the Duo to pull buyers toward the very top of Apple's lineup.
Apple's move toward a more expensive iPhone comes as the economics of the broader smartphone market become increasingly difficult.
Consumers are already holding on to phones for longer, and global smartphone growth is slowing.
Wayne Lam, an analyst at TechInsights, said moving the iPhone further upmarket gives Apple another way to protect the revenue generated by its most important product.
"Given that the iPhone is almost 20 years old, there really isn't anywhere else to head to, given Apple's market position," Lam told CNBC.
With smartphone sales expected to slow, he said, "moving upmarket allows Apple to maintain the all-important iPhone revenues they report every quarter."
Lam described the Duo as an aspirational or luxury product rather than something designed for the average consumer.

But unlike Apple's Vision products, he believes the foldable phone has a path toward becoming a larger category over time, particularly as artificial intelligence changes how consumers interact with their devices.
The trade-off is that pushing prices higher could also make consumers wait longer to upgrade.

Higher iPhone prices could stretch already-long upgrade cycles even further, Lam said, creating what he described as a potential negative feedback loop: devices become more expensive, consumers hold on to them longer and overall demand falls.
Still, Lam expects demand for the Duo to be high relative to its initially limited supply and said the device could "set the bar for premium iPhones moving forward."
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance, a White House official confirmed to CNBC on Friday.
Earlier Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump told reporters that he had just suggested to Zacharia that she quit.
"I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House.
"'If I were you, I'd reconsider,'" the president said he told Zacharia.
The White House official, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the staffing shake-up, confirmed Fox News' report that Zacharia is "transitioning" out of the press secretary role.

Zacharia's five-day tenure in the Trump administration is shorter than that of Anthony Scaramucci, who in 2017 served as White House communications director for less than 11 days. That length of time became jokingly referred to as a "Scaramucci" and was used to measure the durations of other officials who served briefly.
By that metric, Zacharia lasted one-half of one Scaramucci.
"Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain," Scaramucci said in an X post later Friday.

Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked at Trump Media & Technology Group, had faced widespread criticism in the days since she led a short and shaky first press briefing. She also came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background.
Trump spoke to reporters before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms.

But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters.

In the less than six minutes she spent answering questions, Zacharia revealed that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to step down. That departure, and Zacharia's, follow those of a number of other high-ranking female officials in the Trump administration who have quit or been fired in recent months.
"You know, she's been treated very rough. And she's a nice person," Trump said of Zacharia outside the White House.

He accused the media of treating her "very badly" and said that even Fox News TV host Sean Hannity, a supporter of the administration, was "a little bit tough" on Zacharia during her appearance on his show Thursday night.

Hannity, after calling Zacharia's debut briefing "widely panned," had asked about her past claims about her legal work in light of reports that she never passed a bar exam. Zacharia has defended identifying herself as a lawyer, drawing a distinction between that label and calling herself an "attorney."
Hannity pointed out that Zacharia had called herself an attorney in multiple social media posts. "I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record," she replied.

Trump called Zacharia "an attorney" in his Oct. 9 Truth Social post announcing her selection to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Zacharia's first day was Columbus Day.

White House officials had defended Zacharia earlier this week. "Up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in an X post Wednesday.
"At the end of this second term, she'll be remembered as one of the all-time greats," Cheung wrote.

CNN chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins, however, reported Friday that Trump was "embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia's briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance."

"She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily," Trump said of Zacharia in Friday's remarks outside the White House. "And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.'"
Asked if he would keep her in the role, Trump said, "I'm going to let her make that decision."
Miley Cyrus broke down in tears at her Hollywood Bowl performance Friday night during a moving tribute to her godmother, the late Dolly Parton.

The singer projected a photo of the country music icon as the beginning notes of her iconic song “Jolene” played. The Grammy winner told the crowd that one of the things that inspired her to play the venue was the memory of the only time she was able to sit and enjoy a Parton show at the Hollywood Bowl.

She recalling telling her “Aunt Dolly” that for once, she just wanted to sit in the crowd and enjoy her like everyone else. Cyrus began, “If she had it her way, and she was playing a show, I’d be standing right beside her in a matching costume. And so when I was coming to the show at the Bowl to see her, I said, you know, ‘I would love a night where I can just experience you. I can just enjoy you like the rest of the world has gotten to.'”
The “Flowers” singer said her godmother responded by saying, “Okay, Miley,” but Cyrus joked “that never means okay.”

Instead of having Cyrus onstage to perform alongside her, Parton instead opened the show with “The Best of Both Worlds,” Cryus’ hit track from Hannah Montana: “All of a sudden, Dolly enters, but I hear ‘The Best of Both Worlds.’ Yeah, Dolly opened performing Hannah Montana.”

“But that’s just not the end of that story,” she continued. “And she goes, like a proud aunt, ‘I don’t know if y’all know this, but my goddaughter is Hannah Montana, and she’s actually here tonight, but she’s sitting out in her seat. She didn’t want anyone to bug her. She said she just wanted to watch the show,’ which defeated the entire purpose of the conversation that we had just had, because absolutely no one was aware that I was at the concert until she drew an obnoxious amount of attention to it.”
“But like so many things Dolly did, I didn’t understand at the time,” Cyrus said, adding that she could feel Parton’s presence with her during her Hollywood Bowl performance.

“And I can’t fucking wait because I miss her,” Cyrus said in between tears. “Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced, performed by my Aunt Dolly, and this is one of those songs,” she concluded before launching into a rendition of “Jolene.”

Parton died Aug. 25, after a “brief battle with cancer,” a rep announced. She was 80. Many celebrities paid tribute to the queen of country music after her death, including Cyrus who penned a tribute, writing on Instagram, “The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share.”

“I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis. I will always love her and want to make her proud,” she wrote. “My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things.”
During Cyrus’ Friday night show, she also clutched a frame in the shape of a heart with an image of Parton during “Wrecking Ball,” as that was one of her favorite songs.
The Grammy winner played her first of two shows at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday. Her next performance will be on Sunday. Cyrus recently dropped her 10th studio album Bass Persuades on Sept. 18.
Jacob Elordi thought he was going crazy until he saw a classic John Cassavetes film.

“I probably made three movies that I thought were pretty bad when I was young, and I had hopes and dreams of being this kind of terrific, ferocious stage actor. So I was pretty not fond of myself at that time,” explained the Australian actor during an event presented by Cartier Cinema Club at Santa Monica’s Aero Theatre on Friday. “And I watched this movie and it was one of the first times that I saw the creative process of an actor sort of fleshed out in detail. The movie made me feel a lot less insane and alone.”

It proved to be such a pivotal experience in his creative life that Elordi handpicked that film — 1977’s Opening Night starring Gena Rowlands as a renowned actress teetering on the edge of a breakdown as she inches closer towards big Broadway opening night — for Friday’s screening, which marked the first stateside Cartier Cinema Club event after the initiative’s launch last month at the Venice Film Festival. The luxury house created the initiative to honor the spirit of cinema while paying tribute to artists who make big-screen work. Cartier ambassador Elordi not only selected the film, he sat for a 30-minute discussion about it alongside Oscar-winning filmmaker Sean Baker and moderator Kim Morgan.

Like Rowlands’ character, Myrtle Gordon, Elordi thought he, too, “was having some form of mental breakdown.” But he was able to exhale once he saw how the storyline played out. Rowlands stars alongside Cassavetes, Ben Gazzara, Joan Blondell, Paul Stewart, Zohra Lampert and others.

“This movie showed me that what was actually happening was hopefully the artistic process, the process of creating to a character. You can’t just learn the lines and say the lines. It showed me all the stuff that was going on inside that I thought was sort of my body and mind breaking down [but] was actually a part of the acting process,” explained the Oscar nominated Frankenstein star.

Elordi revealed that he watched Opening Night last week in preparation for today’s event, and he had some similar thoughts to those from his first watch, notably because he’s about to start another new movie shortly that has thrown him for a loop. (Though he didn’t name the project, he’s due to start shooting Ari Aster’s Scapegoat alongside Scarlett Johansson, Jude Law, Ella Purnell and Caleb Landry Jones.)

“I’m getting ready to do a movie now and I’ve been kind of throwing myself on the floor and wondering, should I just drink a lot of vodka? Or should I smash a window? What do I need to do to get to this point?” he wondered aloud. “And me re-watching the film now after making over 10 movies or something like that, again, it invited me back into the creative process and what it means. You can be searching for a character and not know that you’re searching for it. It starts happening in your toes and your knees and your chest. And that’s why I picked this movie because it always makes me feel less crazy and more like I’m actually a part of a process of filmmaking that’s been happening for a long time.”

Morgan, a screenwriter known for work on Nightmare Alley directed by her husband Guillermo del Toro, then asked Elordi if that’s because he’s so absorbed by Rowlands performance. He is and was. “Yeah. I mean the amount of times that I just want to throw myself on the floor and cry and scream and tell the director to go fuck themselves and just drink and drink and drink. It makes me feel a lot less alone as an actor.”

That said, Elordi drew laughs when he said that he had no clue how Rowlands’ pulled off any of her scenes on the big screen, particularly the ones where she was really throwing herself around and acting under the influence. “I don’t know how you do that and not look like a ham because everything she does is so big and so expressive, but it’s all completely contained in truth inside her. I’ve watched that scene so many times. You can spin around in circles until you’re dizzy, you can get drunk, you can do all kinds of things, but I don’t know how she does that. I don’t know how she does anything. She’s a genius.”
Baker then weighed on on Cassavetes’ filmography and how inspired he is by the entirety of his work.

“You get asked often as an independent filmmaker, ‘What is your favorite Cassavetes?’ And it really depends on the day because, first off, they’re all masterpieces. They deal with very personal, universal issues and struggles that we all go through. So it really depends on where you are in your life,” he explained. “It’s where I am in my life and that’s how I gravitates towards a certain title. I said Husbands back in the day because I think that was my guy film. Then when I started exploring genre cinema, I was more drawn towards The Killing of a Chinese Bookie.”

Later, when he started working more with actors and honing his craft as a filmmaker, Baker then leaned more toward A Woman Under the Influence and Opening Night, he said. “I can go on forever about him. He’s basically the godfather of U.S. indie cinema and had really just in many ways I think showed us how to do it.”
Morgan closed the conversation by asking both Elordi and Baker if they take inspiration from the many risks Cassavetes took throughout his career.

“I think all artists should take risks,” said the Anora auteur in answering first. “Obviously he did throughout his entire career, which may be hurt in the moment. He was always ahead of his time, but it also proves one very important thing — that cream rises. We’re here 50 years later talking about this film and celebrating this film? That proves that taking risks, staying true to your own, not compromising, and making art that’s a little unsafe is worth it.”
Baker’s words generated an enthusiastic round of applause.

“[Cassavetes] said something like, ‘I’d love to be part of the studio system and have my rent paid and my family good, but I just can’t do it. I’d love to, but I just can’t do it.’ And that’s my favorite thing about these movies. There was no other story he could have told. It made him too ferocious and angry or upset. There was no other way that he could have made movies,” Elordi added in closing. “In movies now, we need a lot of that. Something that you can’t deny, something that you have to do, no matter if it sends you broke, hungry, tired, jobless, you’ve got to make that movie that you have to make. And that’s exactly what we do.”

Florida is becoming one of the bigger enigmas of the already-puzzling 2026 election season. Democrats are showing themselves to be surprisingly competitive. Democrat David Jolly is running neck-and-neck with Trump-approved Republican Byron Donalds in two of three recent polls for the governor job.

And Jacksonville legislator and DSA member Angie Nixon, having upset moderate Democrat Alex Vindman in the primary, now is at least keeping it close against Republican incumbent Ashley Moody. All of which is startling in a state that went for Donald Trump by 13 points just two years ago and hasn’t elected a Democratic governor since 1994.
Now Nixon is turning up the heat on Republican candidates.

On an upcoming episode of Crooked Media’s YouTube show Long Play, Nixon lets it fly against the Republican gubernatorial candidate. “Byron Donalds doesn’t support Black people,” she tells hosts Jennifer Palmieri and Errin Haines on camera in an early cut of the episode, which debuts Monday. Haines then follows up by asking Nixon to explain what she means when she says that Donalds is “going to bring back the worst parts of our history.” Nixon replies, “I mean, he is someone who said that Black people were better off during the Jim Crow era.”
The race has grown contentious but seems to be reaching a new level of fervor as it heads into the final two weeks.

Nixon has said at rallies that she wants to keep funding the police, referring to a common anti-DSA knock, because she wants Moody, Ron DeSantis and Trump locked up. For his part, vice president J.D. Vance said recently at a rally, addressing Nixon, “Get the hell out of here, you don’t belong in America.” (Nixon in the episode: “They don’t have anything to run on but cruelty.”)

Meanwhile, Donalds has been criticized by Jolly for not extending leniency to young people that he was shown when he was arrested on drug charges as a young man and given the opportunity of a diversion program; a hot-button new ad has a retired U.S. General calling Donalds “weak” and a “hypocrite” for it. (Palmieri and Haines discuss the ad in the new episode.)

Launched earlier this year, Long Play examines the divisions and shifting political alignments in various Southern states. After concluding its first season with trips to Georgia, Texas and other Southern states, the show kicks off its second season ahead of the midterms with a Florida episode.

Five flagship and three bonus episodes are planned, straddling both sides of the midterms and set in Texas and Georgia, where close Senate races are unfolding, among other states. The overall goal remains to recalibrate perceptions of the region as a GOP stronghold, which principals say is far too simplistic and out of date.

In Florida, Donalds has looked to court the Black vote to gain the governorship. “You’ve been faithful to that [Democratic] party, have they been faithful to you?,” he recently told an audience at HBCU Florida A&M. Donalds would be Florida’s first Black governor, though has struggled to gain support of large numbers of Black voters, even losing 17 counties in August’s primary to white opponents.

As for the Senate, flipping a Florida seat blue (the seat Nixon is seeking is currently held by Moody, who was appointed two years ago when Marco Rubio was named Secretary of State), is a nice-to-have for Florida Democrats but not seen as essential in retaking control of the Senate.

Nixon says on the show that she thinks a win for her is viable. “So, honestly, there’s a whole bunch of polls,” says Nixon, as she seeks to become both the first Black senator and first female Democratic Senator in Florida’s history. “There are some ranging from tied to seven points. Recently, one was two, I was two points down, like, yesterday. And so the only poll that matters is the Election Day poll.”

In an email, Palmieri said that “My takeaway is neither party can ever write off Florida. It’s too big, too dynamic to take for granted…any outcome is possible.” Added Haines: “The 2026 midterm cycle has been unpredictable — and Florida is arguably one of the biggest examples of that unpredictability.”

Palmieri, a former Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama comms exec who also cohosted Showtime staple The Circus, and Haines, editor-at-large for The 19th, co-host the show with contributions from former NOLA mayor Mitch Landrieu. Circus producer Left/Right produces, and Crooked Media fixture Jon Favreau exec produces. A companion podcast will also be released.
