Oct. 16 (UPI) -- The Justice Department on Friday reached a settlement with a Mississippi city after a federal investigation found its police department engaged in a pattern of civil rights violations.
The agreement with the city of Lexington requires changes to police policies involving arrests, searches, use of force, fines, fees and bail procedures.
The settlement follows a September 2024 report in which the Justice Department found that the Lexington Police Department engaged in a pattern of violating residents' constitutional rights.
Under the agreement, the city and its police department will revise policies governing traffic and pedestrian stops, searches, arrests and the use of force.
The department will also update how officers report those activities and how their actions are reviewed.
Other changes include revisions to policies involving fines and fees, bail and release criteria, and potential conflicts of interest.
"Today's agreement reflects a shared commitment to meaningful and sustainable change," said U.S. Attorney J.E. Baxter Kruger, of the Southern District of Mississippi, in a statement.

"Through these reforms, we seek not only to address the concerns identified in our investigation, but also to strengthen public trust and promote practices that respect the rights and dignity of every person."
Oct. 16 (UPI) -- A federal appeals court on Friday appeared poised to reject the Trump administration's assertion that a federal law regulating presidential records is unconstitutional.
A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit questioned government lawyers over their attempts to strike down the Presidential Records Act, Politico reported.
Enacted in 1978 following the Watergate scandal, the law says presidential records are government property and must be turned over by the White House to the National Archives.
Trump administration lawyer John Bailey argued the act was an "unconstitutional intrusion on the presidency," The New York Times reported.
Judges on the panel appeared skeptical of the government's position that the records belong to the president.
"Can the president then offer on eBay to sell them, all of our national security secrets, to the highest bidder?" Judge Patricia Millett asked Bailey.
"The Presidential Records Act, if unconstitutional, would not be a bar to that," Bailey replied. "Consistent with history and tradition ... the president's papers belong to the president, yes."
Judge Cornelia Pillard went further, asking Bailey what would happen if the records were inherited by relatives of the president.

"So, the bad boy nephew of the deceased president decides they're going to sell the presidential records to the highest bidder, and that happens to be, you know, the Chinese Communist Party," the judge added.
The Presidential Records Act came into focus when President Donald Trump was accused of keeping classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago residence.
The documents were seized by the FBI in a raid in August 2022.

NEW YORK, Oct. 16 (UPI) -- The Rainmaker Season 2, which premieres on USA Network Friday, finds Milo Callaghan's fledgling attorney Rudy Baylor enjoying the success of his first big courtroom win, but sticking with the struggling law firm that hired him when no one else would.

"It was a smart start to the story. I think lots of people think that when they arrive at or meet their goal, on the other side of that is the oasis, nirvana, ecstasy and, in reality, usually, when you hit the top of the mountain very quickly, you're over the peak and you're going down the other side," Callaghan, 28, told UPI in a recent Zoom interview.

"At the end of Season 1, he achieves everything that he set out to achieve in a professional and personal sense. He loses his relationship, but he builds this new family. He makes all this money for this woman Dot [Karen Bryson] that he loves," the actor explained.
"He finds justice for [Dot's son] Donny Ray, and also, he garners the respect that he feels that he didn't get in that first episode when he comes to the table and John Slattery fired me."

The adaptation of John Grisham's best-selling novel of the same name sees Rudy team up with a ruthless ambulance chaser named Bruiser (Lana Parilla) and Deck, her resourceful paralegal, who can't pass the bar exam (P.J. Byrne).
"She's tough. She's the voice that you don't want to hear, but you need to hear," Callaghan said about Bruiser.

"She's actually a real friend because regardless of whether it feels like she's acting in Rudy's interests, according to Rudy's point of view, she's always acting in Rudy's interests, according to her highest sense of morality and moral character."
Guiding Rudy is the idea that who you fight FOR is more important than a potential payday in deciding whether to take on a new case.
"I can't speak for the writers as to whether or not they meant to explore this, but it's understanding that money is just currency," Callaghan said.
"Money is just a means of measuring value and life is about value exchange and another side of that is time and energy," he added.

"It's this attractive resource that seems to be a sure and fast way to change your circumstances. But, the reality is, people only really want money for the connection that it facades as. I think most people would happily trade all their money for a really good friend or for a good family relationship."
In Season 2, Rudy enlists his former client Dot to help him, Bruiser and Deck get a young boy out of juvenile detention where he is being abused.

"He inherently has this gift of understanding that the relationships of the people around him are most important," Callaghan said. "It's the adage of, 'Did the pirates find the treasure X, or was it the friends they made along the way?' And the reality is that it's almost always the friends."

Slattery plays Leo F. Drummond, managing partner at the powerful law firm where Rudy worked for a few short hours before being canned for challenging the boss during a meeting with the staff, which includes Rudy's girlfriend Sarah (Madison Iseman), who doesn't leave when he does.
Season 1 ended with Sarah blindsiding Rudy during a trial with details about a personal trauma Rudy had shared with her in confidence.
The betrayal understandably led to their breakup.

"We didn't really explore that at the end of last season, this fallout of this relationship that they had, because she had gone so far down the road of this Faustian pact that she'd made that I think she fell out of Rudy's circle," Callaghan said. "He had no interest in talking with her anymore."

Season 2 sees Sarah trying to make amends with Rudy at the bar he bought with his pay from Dot's lawsuit against a hospital that covered up that a nurse on their staff had intentionally killed 15 people.
Instead of responding to her heartfelt speech, Rudy simply replies, "We're closed," as Deck listens in without Sarah knowing.
"It's the best, right? That's all credence to the writers and Michael [Seitzman's] vision," Callaghan said.

"A lot of people have said to me that that's their favorite scene and I think that all I did was look at Maddie and be with her and she really carried that," he added. "I was given the gift of just reacting that day. I think she did a really special job."
Merle Dandridge joins the cast season as Sarah's new employer, Amanda Vonn.
"It's hard to beat John Slattery from last year and I know that that casting process was a long, tough one," Callaghan said.

"Michael and the producers found Merle, who is just phenomenal and such a graceful, warm presence on set, such a giving actress that it was really a joy to work with her and just cool to see her do her thing," he added. "She breathed life into that character. I'm really excited for people to see her."
Before being fired five days into her stint as White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia spent much of the day attempting to explain her past.

Throughout her brief tenure, Zacharia’s résumé was the source of much intrigue. Foremost was the fact that despite claiming to be an attorney for much of her career, she never actually passed the California bar, as she was eventually forced to admit. Another element of her professional history, WIRED reported, was a role as an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, a fitness multilevel marketing company.

WIRED has now uncovered new details of her relationship to an AI-powered rare-earth mining operation called NRED Intelligent Mining, which counts former Department of Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem as a strategic adviser.

On June 24, NRED—then known as NovaRed Mining, a small copper-and-gold exploration company in Vancouver, Canada—issued a press release to share that Zacharia, who had left a role as a DHS spokesperson two months before, was joining the advisory board alongside Noem.

In her new role, according to the release, Zacharia would provide “strategic guidance” to NovaRed’s board of directors as it advanced exploration projects, as well as “emerging artificial intelligence initiatives.”

It does not appear, though, that she ever worked there. When asked on Friday whether she was still on the board, she said, “That was fake,” and referred WIRED to Sam Amsterdam, a “strategic marketing and media engagement professional” whose clients have included the government of Kazakhstan and political parties in Georgia, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe.

“That release was not approved by Ms. Zacharia and was issued without her consent,” says Amsterdam, whose brother is listed as a member of NRED management on the company’s website and said he was speaking as a friend and colleague of Zacharia, not a representative. “I know all that to be factual.” He quickly added that while there had been discussions of her joining the company, she hadn’t actually done so.

Valentin Saitarli, who was NRED’s chief technology officer and says he is onboarding as CEO, confirmed that there were discussions about a role but said that it “never materialized,” adding, “It was a bit like signing up for a gym but never actually going for a workout.” Describing NRED, Saitarli says, “We go full robots and AI.”

Despite Amsterdam’s understanding that it had been withdrawn, the press release claiming Zacharia was joining the company remained on NRED’s website as of Friday. An archived version of the website showed Zacharia listed as management as of at least July.
When WIRED asked Saitarli about this, he said that the site was being updated.

Zacharia, whose NovaRed role was announced eight days after Noem’s appointment was announced, worked under Noem as DHS’s deputy assistant press secretary for public affairs for about a month and was reported to have close ties with de facto DHS chief of staff Corey Lewandowski. (She denied any such ties to The Daily Mail.)

The announcement that Noem was joining the advisory board of a Canadian mining company triggered an outcry among Canadians, who pointed to statements she had made referring to Canada as the “51st state.” At that time, The Globe and Mail described NovaRed as “a copper and gold exploration company that generates no revenue.” The paper noted that in January, NoraRed was holding only $65,689 in cash, which the company said “wouldn’t be enough to cover all of its expected expenses for the next 12 months.”

But around the spring, something changed. NovaRed began stacking its advisory board not with geologists and technical consultants—which would be typical for a junior mining company—but with heavy hitters with ties to the defense sector, MAGA, and other international entities.

Earlier this month, NRED announced that it was pivoting away from its flagship Wilmac Copper-Gold Project and is putting all its resources into developing and commercializing “MetalCore,” its “AI-assisted mineral exploration platform.”

“I want to build a new generation of robotics and mining,” Saitarli tells WIRED. “Do we want to get stuck in the Stone Age or horses age? No, we want to live on Mars, spend time in hotels in space, have a wedding party on the moon … We will bring robotics and AI to global mining and beyond our planet, hopefully.”

Phil Ehr, a retired US Navy commander who is running for Congress as a Democrat in Florida, was brought into NovaRed earlier this year. “I know nothing about mining. I know nothing about commodities,” Ehr tells WIRED in a phone call. “But I do know that we need more copper. I do know that we need more critical minerals.” He had only been at the company for a couple of months when, he said, he was blindsided by NovaRed’s announcement that Kristi Noem and “another DHS spokesperson”—whom he recalls being Zacharia—had also been brought onto the advisory board.
“To the best of my knowledge, [Zacharia] came at the same time as Kristi Noem did without any consultation to me and was just like, boom, there,” recalls Ehr.

Noem, who did not immediately reply to requests for comment, was fresh off overseeing the disastrous ICE occupation in Minneapolis, and Ehr didn’t want to be associated with her. “So I asked the company, “Why is Kristi Noem here? I just can't work with her because she is so controversial. We are on different sides of what's right and wrong in, in the federal government,” says Ehr.

He thought it was odd that NovaRed seemed to be stacking its ranks with people who, like him, didn’t know very much about the mining industry. He expected some geologists in the mix, or technical consultants. Instead, some of the other people hired included Gregory Fedun, who previously “served as a key advisor to the United Arab Emirates’ Al Mualla Royal Family on a range of international projects,” and media executive Lee Caplin, coproducer of HBO’s True Detective series. Ehr resigned from the advisory board not long after Noem joined.

While she was attempting to clarify the nature of her relationship to NRED, Zacharia was also tending to other matters. On Thursday evening, while she still held her position as White House press secretary, Zacharia reached out to a WIRED reporter to suggest they contact fitness influencer named Jenelle Summers for “clarity” on Beachbody, the MLM she was previously affiliated with and which Summer brought her into.

Summers said she didn’t recall much about Zacharia—whom, she said, she met online—other than that “she was always kind to me and someone that was into fitness and believed in the products and programs.”

“To my recollections,” she added, “she didn't do much with it.” Summers rejected the idea that she had been involved in a “pyramid scheme,” which is how Zacharia had characterized the company to WIRED. ”That's kind of old-school thinking,” Summers said. “It was a network marketing business model.”
“I don't have any comment on that other than to say she's always been kind to me,” Summers said when asked what she made of Zacharia’s rise to prominence.
Zacharia did not respond to requests for comment on her firing. When asked if he had comment on her having been let go, Amsterdam told a WIRED reporter, “Well, that’s news to me!”

Chicago-area law enforcement officers took part in an undercover probe by Immigration and Customs Enforcement into Minneapolis mutual aid networks last spring as part of the feds’ conspiracy investigation into 15 Twin Cities activists facing federal felony charges for resisting Operation Metro Surge, according to newly released documents reviewed by WIRED.

An April report by ICE’s investigations wing, Homeland Security Investigations, titled “Antifa Roadshow,” details in-person and electronic surveillance by a joint task force of an April 2 talk. The task force was made up of 14 law enforcement officers—six local cops and eight HSI Chicago agents. The talk included self-described anarchists in Minnesota who spoke about their organizing experiences during the three-month immigration surge, which resulted in the killings of two US citizens.

The document, released by the 15 Minnesota activists’ defense team as part of the ongoing federal case against them, exposes close cooperation between local police, sheriffs, and HSI agents on a prosecution that critics say crosses the line into political repression. The Chicago HSI task force, which included officers from Chicago, Aurora, Downer’s Grove, Cook County, and Kane County, used two undercover agents, unspecified electronic surveillance, audio recordings, license-plate-reader data, and surveillance cameras from Chicago’s sprawling CCTV network to identify the April 2 event’s attendees and build connections to other anti-ICE protests in Illinois and other states.

Records produced by the Kane County Sheriff’s office show the unit in question is the Chicago-area Homeland Security Investigations Task Force. Local cops who join the unit are accepted on either a full- or part-time basis for two years, with the sign-off of their superiors.

Since Operation Midway Blitz in Illinois last autumn, residents in Chicago and surrounding communities have pressed elected officials for answers about cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE. While Illinois state law prevents local law enforcement from participating in immigration enforcement operations, criminal investigations by HSI appear to fall outside those restrictions because they pertain to ICE’s other law enforcement functions.

Chicago police have substantial approval requirements for surveilling and infiltrating protests or public gatherings, per a 2017 departmental order. It is unclear how these regulations apply to Chicago Police Department agents participating in joint task forces with federal agencies.

In response to questions from WIRED, the CPD claims that no First Amendment notifications to CPD’s chain of command or the department’s general counsel were made for the April 2 investigation, and says its work with HSI is permitted under Illinois law because it pertained to criminal enforcement, not immigration. A source with knowledge of the matter stated that CPD believed the early April surveillance operation was in service of a federal racketeering investigation. The only financial element mentioned in the report is a GoFundMe account to support the Crimethinc speaking tour. There is no mention of funds solicited or received at the April 2 event.

The Chicago Mayor’s Office did not provide comment ahead of publication. In response to queries from WIRED, ICE would neither confirm nor deny details of past or present investigations and said individual agents are not authorized to speak to the media.

HSI is also emerging as the point agency for Trump’s war on internal dissent and opposition politicians: Its agents, not the FBI, conducted the Minnesota 15 investigation and served a search warrant earlier this month on congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

The targeted April 2 event was held at Co-Prosperity, a Leftist gallery in the Southside Chicago neighborhood of Bridgeport. Several speakers from the Twin Cities area attended the event to share information about resisting federal immigration surges. This was part of a national tour last spring that was organized by the longtime anarchist collective Crimethinc, whose meetings have been infiltrated by federal informants repeatedly over the decades and contributed to the convictions of Eric McDavid, as well as 2008 Republican National Convention protester Matthew DePalma.

Per the four-page HSI report, a plainclothes cop from suburban Aurora was dropped off at the Co-Prosperity event by Officer Mike Xu from the wealthy village of Downers Grove; HSI undercover agent #9147 walked in five minutes later, once the undercover cop from Aurora confirmed no security checks were done at the door.

The undercover HSI agent transmitted a live recording of the event to the rest of the surveillance team for an hour, until transmission was lost. The recordings of the incident were uploaded and shared with HSI agent Kenneth Popovits, a financial crimes investigations supervisor who was working on a temporary assignment in Minneapolis.

Remarks by defendant Callum Robinet from the April 2 talk in Bridgeport about building rapid-response networks are included in the federal conspiracy indictment brought against the Minnesota 15, implicating the Chicagoland law enforcement that participated in surveillance in the controversial prosecution.
The Aurora Police Department, Downer’s Grove Police Department, and Kane County Sheriff did not respond to requests for comment.

The HSI Chicago surveillance team logged 219 vehicles parked in the vicinity of Co-Prosperity. Several subjects already under investigation, including some of the speakers on the tour, were identified by ICE. Ryan Wasson, a Kane County Sheriff’s deputy, spotted a hooded, masked man outside the venue removing an object from his trunk. Running the license plate, Wasson identified the man as the subject of an October 4 arrest during Operation Midway Blitz whose prosecution had been declined by assistant US attorney Christopher Veatch.

Outside the venue, agents Joel Sullivan and Michael Finerty spotted an unnamed subject already under investigation for running “an anti-ICE Signal chat and group called ‘ICE Cream Patrol’” and noted an orange Hyundai had been documented near two March 2026 protests outside the ICE detention center in Broadview, Illinois. The surveillance lasted for roughly two hours until 8:30 pm local time on April 2.

Nick Nunez, a veteran Chicago Police detective detailed to the joint task force, filed a request to obtain surveillance footage from a CPD camera outside the venue; the request would take a week to complete, and it is unclear whether he received footage. All information obtained during the April investigation in Chicago was shared with HSI St. Paul/Minnesota, according to the agency’s report.

Ed Yohnka, a spokesman for the American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois, calls the surveillance of the Bridgeport gathering “very troubling,” adding that local law enforcement should make a full accounting of their role in the incident and participation in joint task forces with federal agencies.

“No one should be subjected to surveillance and infiltration by law enforcement simply for engaging in constitutionally protected activity, including the ability to gather together and express dissatisfaction with public policy,” Yohnka says. “It is also a moment for local law enforcement to reexamine their participation in task forces with the Trump administration, especially any group focused on combatting ‘terrorism.’”

The April 2 meeting in Bridgeport is not the only out-of-state gathering spied upon by HSI during the Minnesota 15 investigation. Reports obtained by defense attorneys through discovery show that events on the same Crimethinc tour in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and Seattle, Washington, were monitored in person by local HSI agents, who reported the speech’s contents back to their colleagues in Minneapolis.

Rembrandt van Rijn’s most famous paintings—such as The Night Watch and The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp—may represent his 17th-century Dutch surroundings. But the artist’s well of inspiration reached deep into antiquity, tapping sources like the Old Testament and Greek myth.

A newly announced Rembrandt exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York will dissect the artist’s unique relationship with stories and artistic traditions of the past. “Rembrandt and the Ancients,” opening in November 2027, will feature more than 125 artworks, including around 70 Rembrandt paintings, prints and drawings displayed alongside ancient and Renaissance artifacts.

“As the Met’s first major exhibition dedicated to Rembrandt’s work in 20 years, ‘Rembrandt and the Ancients’ offers new possibilities for understanding one of the world’s most iconic artists,” says museum director and CEO Max Hollein in a statement. Several of the pieces coming to the Met have never been seen in the United States before.

One piece on display will be Rembrandt’s The Abduction of Ganymede (1635), depicting the myth of a young Trojan boy who is kidnapped by Zeus, disguised as an eagle. Another, Bathsheba Holding King David’s Letter (1654), shows the eponymous biblical character—a serial Rembrandt subject—holding a letter from King David, who in the Old Testament observes her bathing on her roof and forces her into adultery.

Such timeless tales have inspired many artists throughout history, including Renaissance masters like Michelangelo and Leonardo da Vinci. Rembrandt’s own fascination with antiquity was partially inspired by such artworks, an art historical connection that the exhibition will outline by including Renaissance objects alongside the Dutch master’s paintings.

One Rembrandt painting included in “Rembrandt and Ancients” is itself a meditation on inspiration across centuries. In Aristotle with a Bust of Homer (1653), the fourth-century-B.C.E. philosopher contemplates the author of the Odyssey, who lived centuries before Aristotle was born.

“Rembrandt and the Ancients” explores “this relationship between tradition and innovation and this idea of the past as a lens for the present,” exhibition co-curator Joanna Sheers Seidenstein tells the New York Times’ Leila Sheridan.

Rembrandt’s classically-inspired paintings are identifiable by his style of dramatic light, shadow and emotional depth. Seidenstein singles out Bathsheba Holding King David’s Letter for its subject’s facial expression, telling the Times that it is “a masterpiece of painting and one of the artist’s most affecting treatments of emotion and psychological interiority.”

That painting will be displayed alongside an ancient Roman relief and a print that inspired Rembrandt’s work. Also on display will be Rembrandt’s interpretation of the myth of Diana and Actaeon, famously depicted by Renaissance master Titian, as well as a red chalk drawing of the biblical King Solomon.

During Rembrandt’s lifetime, there was a “flourishing interest in antiquity” in the Dutch Republic, per the statement. In 17th-century Amsterdam, the elite collected ancient art, staged classical dramas and translated ancient texts into Dutch. Rembrandt’s interpretations of ancient stories and characters often articulated ideas about his own era. “He produced highly distinctive imagery that is at once playful and poignant, irreverent and intense—and always supremely human,” according to the statement.
- Let the Little Children Come Unto Me is a 17th-century painting of a biblical scene which experts believe was started by Rembrandt and finished by another artist.
- A recent restoration revealed Rembrandt’s original unfinished work.

Many of the exhibition’s pieces belong to the Louvre Museum, which is co-organizing the exhibition with the Met. “Rembrandt and the Ancients” will travel to Paris for a run at the Louvre in the spring of 2028.

“Uniting masterpieces from the Met collection with spectacular international loans, the exhibition brings together an unprecedented and powerful ensemble that reveals the depth of Rembrandt’s vision,” Hollein says in the statement.
“Rembrandt and the Ancients” will be on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York from November 7, 2027, until February 6, 2028.

Welsh folklore tells of a Roman emperor named Macsen Wledig, who was tormented by visions of a beautiful stranger in a faraway land. According to a 19th-century translation of the Mabinogion, a collection of 11 medieval tales, “Except when he slept, he saw nothing of her, for he knew not where in the world she was.”

Macsen’s quest to uncover this mystery woman’s identity eventually leads him to the British Isles, where his beloved lives with her family. In return for her hand in marriage, the soon-to-be empress asks Macsen to conquer “the island of Britain for her father, from the Channel to the Irish Sea, together with three adjacent islands.” Macsen eagerly complies, making his way to the top of Frenni Fawr, a peak in what is now Pembrokeshire, Wales. Per the Mabinogion, “There the emperor pitched his tent. And that encamping place is called Cadair Maxen, even to this day.”

Historians have long known that this legendary figure was inspired by an actual ancient ruler: Magnus Maximus, a general whose troops proclaimed him Roman emperor in the West in the late fourth century C.E. But the events described in the Mabinogion have largely been consigned to folklore—until now.

As Dalya Alberge reports for the Guardian, an ongoing excavation led by Mark Merrony, an archaeologist at the University of Oxford in England, has unearthed remnants of a Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, including fourth-century coins, an iron stylus, a game piece and fragments of ceramic tiles. The finds bolster Merrony’s argument that the Romans played a greater role in the region’s ancient past than previously believed.

“If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” Merrony tells the Guardian. “It’s such a remote area, but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.”

Merrony stumbled upon the fort while riding his bike in north Pembrokeshire in 2024. “Sticking out of the ground was a triangular piece that looked like a Roman roofing slate,” he told the Pembrokeshire Herald’s Tom Sinclair at the time. “I pulled it up, and lo and behold, it’s an archetypal Roman roofing slate,” with a hexagonal shape and a long point. Early investigations indicate that the stronghold stretched over as many as three hectares, meaning it could have housed around 500 soldiers.

In the two years since Merrony’s initial discovery, the archaeologist has conducted a geophysical survey and trial excavations at the site. He and his colleagues had a “breakthrough” in early September, when they found “bases of floor structures built of clay and packed with the remnants of thin stone blocks,” as well as traces of a Roman road, a kiln, flooring consistent with a Roman granary, and assorted artifacts such as pottery shards and a spindle whorl, Merrony writes for the Conversation. The finds support the theory that the site was once home to a timber auxiliary fort.

Merrony doesn’t suggest that Maximus himself constructed the fort. Instead, he argues that Sextus Julius Frontinus, a Roman governor of Britain, established it between 74 and 78 C.E. Maximus could have used the site centuries later.

“The Roman army were very regimented and always dug a trench around their camp in the shape of a playing card,” Merrony tells the BBC program “Newsround.” “If you’re spending a couple of nights somewhere, it takes an awful lot of effort and labor. But if there’s a fort a couple of miles away that’s clearly visible from the peak of the mountain—which it is and would have been—[Maximus] would have not only been able to see it but would have known about it.” As Merrony writes for the Conversation, “The discovery represents an extraordinary fusion between myth and reality and demonstrates that folklore is often underpinned by fact.”

- In the late third century C.E., the Roman emperor Diocletian established a power-sharing system known as the tetrarchy, essentially separating the empire into divisions overseen by different rulers. The East-West split became official in 395 C.E., when the two sons of Theodosius I each inherited one half of the empire.

- “The ideal was of two parts ruling in harmony,” Mark Humphries, a classicist at Swansea University in Wales, told Live Science’s Joe Phelan in 2022. “That said, there were moments of tension. On occasion, relations could break down.”

Maximus was a Spaniard who commanded Roman soldiers in their fight against the Picts and the Scots. In 383 C.E., Maximus’ men named him Western emperor in place of Gratian, the unpopular ruler who officially held the title. Although Gratian attempted to reclaim power, he was no match for Maximus on the field of battle, and the usurper was soon able to solidify his claim to the throne.

Maximus set his sights even higher, however, challenging Gratian’s co-emperor, Valentinian II. That’s when Theodosius I, the duo’s counterpart in the east, decided to intervene. Theodosius defeated Maximus, who was captured and executed in 388 C.E.

So, how did Maximus become Macsen? The 12th-century English chronicler Geoffrey of Monmouth fictionalized Maximus’ life in his History of the Kings of Britain, which depicts the emperor becoming the Christian king of Britain after marrying a Welsh princess traditionally identified as Elen Luyddog.

Maximus’ status as a “Christian Roman Celt” made him “a bridge between the old order in Wales and the new,” the Welsh politician and author Gwynfor Evans wrote in a 1983 essay. “The quite romantic story of Magnus Maximus was transformed by professional Welsh raconteurs, giving Macsen Wledig, emperor of Rome, a place in our legend second only to Arthur.”

When Jackie, a beloved bald eagle who captured hearts across the country thanks to a livestream of her nest, died in August after several weeks in intensive care at the Ojai Raptor Center in California, experts were baffled by what had caused her mysterious illness. Now, a necropsy has revealed that bird flu was to blame, according to an October 14 statement from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).
The finding has caught scientists by surprise and underscores how the illness is causing devastation among wildlife populations across the United States.

Bird flu, or highly pathogenic avian influenza, is a contagious viral disease. As implied, it primarily spreads among birds, but one strain of the virus, H5N1, has been wreaking havoc in other animals, including dairy cows and wild mammals, in recent years. It has even reached isolated regions like Tasmania, Iceland and Antarctica. In rare cases, humans can also contract this strain of bird flu; symptoms include eye redness, a cough and a sore throat.

Eagles aren’t natural hosts for the virus. They’re usually exposed to it through contact with infected birds, common carriers being waterfowl and shorebirds, or by eating infected prey. While bird flu was spreading among bald eagles in 2022, when more than 300 of the raptors tested positive for the illness, there isn’t currently an outbreak among the animals. That’s why experts are surprised by the cause of Jackie’s death.

“Nobody knew this was even a probability,” says William Bowerman, a wildlife ecologist at the University of Maryland, to Jeanine Santucci at USA Today. In the spring, California even declared that bird flu was no longer impacting the state’s poultry industry, he adds. “Her case gave us more science than we were expecting.”

Jackie hatched in the spring of 2012 in Big Bear Valley, California. A few years later, the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley installed a camera near her parents’ nest, which Jackie eventually took over. Viewers followed along as she and her recent mate, Shadow, raised chicks and carried out their daily activities among the San Bernardino Mountains. They became internet stars during the Covid-19 pandemic.
This past July, however, Jackie was taken to the Ojai Raptor Center after she was seen in a ground fight with two young eagles. She was unable to fly.

“The adult eagle that we picked up was sick, very sick,” a San Dimas Raptor Rescue official told KCAL News’ Dean Fioresi at the time. “There were no physical injuries, so we were able to do a quick assessment; look at her wings and stuff like that. There was nothing obvious, but she was very skinny and underweight.”
Experts deemed that she had probably been ill for a while. Still, Jackie’s symptoms were unusual for bird flu.

“In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia and the development of bacterial sepsis,” says Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, in the statement.
“You would not expect that bird flu would have been the cause for her decline just based on her symptoms,” Bowerman tells USA Today.
No evidence currently suggests that Shadow or the eaglets are sick.

While there are still unanswered questions surrounding Jackie’s death, like how she contracted the virus in the first place, one thing is clear: She continues to have an impact. “The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds,” says CDFW Director Meghan Hertel in the statement.

“We’re grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being,” she adds. “Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future.”
Jackie was cremated following the investigation to prevent the transmission of the illness.

Archaeologists digging at a 13,800-year-old site in interior Alaska have unearthed thousands of artifacts and fossils, including what may be the bones of the earliest domesticated dogs in the Americas, the earliest needles and dwellings in the Western Hemisphere, and stone tools that reveal cultural connections across the Bering Land Bridge.

At a site called Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ (which means "They Were There" in the Alaska Native Athabascan language), about 34 miles (55 kilometers) southeast of Fairbanks, archaeologists have excavated an encampment that some of the first people to settle in North America used off and on for a millennium.

Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ is located in eastern Beringia, the geographical region that connected northeast Asia and northwest North America during the last ice age. The most recent archaeological and genetic studies suggest that the ancestors of today's Indigenous Americans entered the continent around 21,000 years ago. But since Beringian sites are often the remains of small seasonal hunting camps and are scattered across a large geographic area, much is still unknown about the earliest people who called the Western Hemisphere home.

"I expected we'd find hunting tools and knapping [stone tool making] debris surrounding a hearth or two, but I had no idea that we'd stumble into a base camp with tens of thousands of artifacts," study first author Kelly Graf, an archaeologist at the University of Kansas, told Live Science in an email. "It was a total surprise!"

In a study published Wednesday (Oct. 14) in the journal Science Advances, Graf and co-authors detailed their discoveries at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ, focusing on the earliest occupation, which occurred around 13,800 years ago, as evidence of people "settling in" to their new territory.

The researchers found a hearth, a small pit, and a dirt stain where a wooden post had once stood, likely the remains of a lean-to or early tent house. Additionally, the archaeologists unearthed stone tools, bone needles and a pendant made from an antler. Nearby, they found an earth oven, which was full of charcoal and animal bones and was likely used to slow-cook meat for a large family group.

"The complex feature at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ represents the earliest potential case of a habitation structure in North America," the researchers wrote in the study. "Early Alaskans knew their surroundings well."

The archaeologists were also surprised by the stone tools recovered at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ because they are distinctively shaped and unique to central Alaska. Known as diamond-shaped hafted bifaces, the tools were crafted from rhyolite and basalt and are similar to those typically found much farther west in Beringia, in modern-day northern Siberia. Additionally, obsidian artifacts discovered at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ reveal that people brought the volcanic rock to the site from a geological source hundreds of miles to the northwest.

Bones from more than a dozen wolf-like animals suggest a further connection to Asia, according to the researchers. An analysis of the jaw of one of the animals showed that it was not from a dire wolf (Aenocyon dirus) or from a Pleistocene Beringian or gray wolf (Canis lupus sp.) but rather a population of wolf-like animals unique to central Alaska. Current genetic evidence suggests that early domesticated dogs in North America came from Siberian wolves. The timing and geographical location of Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ provides circumstantial evidence that the people may have been dog owners.
"Like humans, potentially, the canids of Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ and other early Alaskan sites were recent immigrants from Asian Beringia," the researchers wrote.
Although Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ reveals a relationship with sites in Asia, there is also evidence of connections with early American sites south of the Canadian ice sheets, according to the study.

One clue to these connections is the presence of bone artifacts in a sewing kit. The archaeologists found eight bone needle fragments at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ. Previously, the only recovered eyed needles had come from Paleoindian sites in temperate North America. Therefore, the needles from Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ are the oldest needles ever discovered in the Western Hemisphere, and they reveal connections with sites farther south, according to the study.

Another clue is the pendant, which was crafted from antler. The pendant had a hole drilled at one end and was fashioned into a point at the other end. This piece of ancient jewelry is similar to personal adornment items found farther south in North America.

"The co-occurrence of these cultural features at the single site of Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ is truly notable," the researchers wrote, and they "highlight the strong cultural connection between early Beringians and Americans."

It is still unclear whether the people at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ were traveling to make these connections. "It would be hard to pin down whether or not they were moving back and forth during a lifetime, but at least we can say there is a connection," Graf said.

Future excavations in Beringia could help archaeologists learn more about the earliest people in the Americas, according to Graf. "Alaska is a big place and so remote, so there are really just a few small areas that have been intensively investigated," she said.

Spencer Pelton, an archaeologist at the University of Wyoming who was not involved in the research, wrote in an accompanying perspective published in the journal Science Advances that early Indigenous sites in Beringia are key to understanding the peopling of the Americas.

"Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ is remarkable because it is the oldest site in the Americas containing a large and rich assemblage of features, artifacts, and faunal refuse indicative of prolonged residential occupation, providing an unprecedented glimpse into the lives of North America's first residents," Pelton wrote.

Graf is already planning future archaeological excavations in the area. "We're hoping to bring some younger Alaska Native folks out with us in the coming summers," she said, as incorporating local knowledge is important to the project. "Two of our co-authors are elders from Alaska Native corporations nearest to the site," she said. Elders named the Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ site and have visited it to discuss where to excavate and what the archaeologists might find.

There is much left to learn about what was happening in Beringia 14,000 years ago, the researchers wrote, particularly since there are currently only two archaeological sites — including the 24,000-year-old Bluefish Caves site in the Yukon — that suggest humans were settling in Beringia considerably earlier.

"Necklaces" of ultracold atoms have provided new evidence to support a nearly 100-year-old quantum theory.

In 1931, physicists were trying to use quantum mechanics to explain why some materials are magnetic. Then, a young physicist named Hans Bethe looked at a single row of electrons. Each electron's spin can point up or down. Bethe worked out the math for how such a row behaves and found that if a few spins in the row flip, they can stick together and travel down the row as a single unit.

Decades later, physicists found that Bethe's method also works for larger particles moving along a line, such as atoms. If those particles attract each other, the math predicts they will bind into clusters called Bethe strings.
Now, physicists have found evidence of these clusters in a line of ultracold atoms. The findings were published Aug. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The discovery may not create new gadgets, but it addresses a fundamental mystery in physics. Everything around us, from magnets to phone chips, consists of countless interacting particles. This makes their behavior difficult to predict. Ultracold atoms serve as a clear and adjustable way to study these complex systems.
Researchers have spotted small Bethe strings before, in magnetic crystals and superconducting quantum circuits — but those experiments captured strings one at a time.

Theory predicts that crowds of strings, in many sizes, can change how an entire system behaves, and studying that idea requires making many strings at once. That has been hard to do with atoms. Atoms that attract each other usually collapse into a clump. But this time, the team appears to have made many strings of different sizes at once, including some with more than six atoms.

It's tricky to get atoms to attract each other. In three dimensions, a gas made of attracting atoms tends to collapse as the atoms clump together and form molecules. That process releases energy that kicks atoms out of the experiment, so the gas quickly collapses and disappears. But when they're in a single line, the atoms behave differently.

"They are really a bit like pearls on a string, right? Like on a necklace, they cannot go past," study co-author Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, an experimental physicist at the University of Innsbruck, told Live Science. "In 3D, everything would collapse. But in 1D, it does not collapse."

To build their "necklaces," the team started with tens of thousands of cesium atoms cooled into a Bose-Einstein condensate — a state of matter in which atoms chilled to near absolute zero share a single quantum state. Laser beams then divided the condensate into thousands of thin tubes, each of which held up to a few dozen atoms in a line.
At first, the atoms repelled each other. The researchers used a magnetic field to gradually turn that repulsion down to zero, and then turned it into attraction.

The team couldn't see the strings directly. Instead, they let the atoms go and measured how fast the cloud spread. When the atoms could expand only along their tubes, any strings stayed intact. When the atoms were freed in all three dimensions, the strings broke apart and released their binding energy as motion. The researchers found that the 3D clouds spread with about three times as much energy as the one-dimensional ones did.

From that difference, the team estimated how tightly the atoms had been bound. The answer pointed to strings of at least six atoms. The measurements also closely matched predictions from a theory called generalized hydrodynamics, which describes a gas like this one as a fluid made of many kinds of particles, including strings of different sizes. It also tracks how each kind flows over time rather than following every atom.
Nägerl was careful not to call this proof. "That some theory fits to your data is not a proof that something exists," he said; it's just more evidence to support it.

The strings likely don't survive long. Up close, the atoms still feel the three-dimensional world, and the strings eventually decay into ordinary cesium molecules. In the coldest runs, the team lost about 40% of the atoms.
"Transiently you create these Bethe string states," Nägerl said. "But I don't think they are long-lived."

He has an idea for future experiments. Physicists recently learned to shield ultracold molecules with microwaves, which keeps the molecules from colliding at close range. Strings made from shielded molecules might last long enough to be studied directly. But Nägerl stressed that the idea is untested. "I've had nobody do a theory check on my claims now, but I think intuitively this should work," he said.
Another option is quantum gas microscopy, which images atoms one at a time and could offer more direct evidence of individual strings.

For Nägerl, Bethe strings are one step in understanding how quantum systems with many particles behave and settle down over time. His long-term goal is an experiment in which physicists control both how every particle moves and how its spin flips, letting them assemble model materials piece by piece, "like a LEGO type," he said. His team has begun the next step: using lasers to control the spins of the atoms in its one-dimensional gas. He described Bethe strings as "a little diversion." But because the strings form whenever the atoms attract, they can't be ignored.

The fifth-generation Ram 2500 places substantial demands on its brakes. Many of these trucks carry heavy payloads, tow trailers or operate in fleets, so a successful brake job requires a complete-system inspection and parts that match the platform’s thermal and mechanical demands.

This Brake Job covers the 2019-present fifth-generation Ram 2500, not the Ram 1500. The 2500 uses heavy-duty components and platform-specific procedures. Confirm the model year, engine, axle and options before ordering parts or applying specifications.
The Ram 2500 has four-wheel vented discs and dual-piston sliding calipers. Separate parking-brake shoes act against a drum surface inside each rear rotor hat.

Booster configuration depends on the engine. The 6.4L Hemi uses a dual-diaphragm vacuum booster and an electric vacuum pump near the left front of the engine to supplement engine vacuum. The PCM commands the pump based on operating inputs. The 6.7L diesel uses Hydro-Boost, supplied by the power-steering pump, with an accumulator providing limited reserve assist if pump pressure is lost.

When it’s practical, begin the process with a road test and note pedal travel, assist, pull, vibration and noise under normal braking. Confirm the complaint before disassembly; a vibration blamed on the front brakes may originate at the rear, and an assist complaint may come from the vacuum or power-steering circuit rather than the foundation brakes.

Clean around the master-cylinder cap and verify that the fluid is at the MAX mark. On a diesel vehicle, you should also inspect the power-steering fluid level, hoses and lines, because Hydro-Boost depends on that circuit. Low fluid, leaks, restrictions or weak pump output can create assist complaints. On gasoline models, inspect booster vacuum plumbing and electric-pump operation.

Compare inner and outer pad wear and both sides of each axle. Uneven wear can reveal seized hardware, binding pads, piston trouble or slide problems. Replace pads as an axle set if usable lining at the thinnest point is 1 mm (0.04 inch) or less. Inspect boots, pistons, slides, hoses and bleeders for damage, leakage and corrosion.

Be sure to measure the rotors. Minimum thickness is 37.4 mm (1.47 inches) front and 32.4 mm (1.28 inches) rear. Maximum runout is 0.020 mm (0.0008 inch); maximum loose-rotor thickness variation is 0.008 mm (0.00031 inch). You should also inspect the internal parking-brake surface; maximum drum diameter is 207.2 mm (8.157 inches).

Support the caliper and adapter; never let the hose carry their weight. Clean the pad lands and hub face without removing base metal. Install new anti-rattle clips, verify free pad movement and make sure both pistons retract smoothly. Because the rotor fits over the hub studs, hub cleanliness and uniform wheel-fastener torque are critical to controlling installed runout.

Rear service adds the parking-brake assembly. A rotor that will not release may be hanging on the shoes, so release the pedal and back off the star wheel if necessary. With the rotor off, inspect the shoes, springs, adjuster, cable action and drum surface. Clean the hub and bracket, verify piston and slide movement, and install new hardware and sealing washers as required.
Always replace caliper hardware; old clips can restrict pad movement and cause uneven wear.

Use fresh fluid meeting SAE J1703-F and DOT 3 standards. Bleed in this order: right rear, left rear, right front and left front, keeping the reservoir full. For pressure bleeding, use the correct adapter; 15-20 PSI is generally sufficient, depending on equipment limits.

If air entered the HCU, perform a base bleed, use a capable scan tool’s ABS Miscellaneous menu to run the HCU bleed routine, then bleed the base system again. Set the fluid level and verify a firm pedal.

Hydro-Boost is generally self- bleeding. Fill the power-steering reservoir, disable the engine and crank it for several seconds, then recheck the level. Re-enable and start the engine, slowly turn lock to lock twice, shut it off and discharge the accumulator with five pedal applications. Restart, repeat two slow lock-to-lock cycles, shut down and correct the level. If the fluid foams, let it dissipate before repeating the final cycles.

Adjust the shoes before cable tension. With the pedal fully released and the front cable slackened at the frame-rail adjuster, turn each star wheel through the backing-plate hole until slight drag is felt, then back it off until drag disappears. Adjust both sides equally.

Cable-tensioner adjustment is normally required only after replacement or disconnection. After verifying cable movement and shoe adjustment, fully apply the pedal. Mark the non-threaded tensioner rod 1/4 inch from the tensioner edge and tighten the nut until the mark disappears. Release the pedal, confirm both wheels rotate freely, verify that the brake holds and road-test the truck.

Super Cruise is GM’s hands-free driver-assistance system, offered on certain 2019-205 GM vehicles. Feature-wise, it combines adaptive cruise control, automatic braking, lane centering, driver monitoring, GPS and high-definition map data.

In the shop, diagnosis starts by separating a component fault or configuration problem from a normal system inhibit. A missing condition or failure in any of the above-mentioned areas can prevent engagement.

On an approved mapped road, Super Cruise uses Adaptive Cruise Control to manage speed and following distance while the lane-control system commands electric power steering to center the vehicle. The forward camera supplies lane information, and Adaptive Cruise Control sensing hardware tracks traffic ahead. The engine and electronic brake control modules carry out acceleration and braking requests. Because these modules exchange network data, a voltage, communication or configuration fault outside the camera can disable the system.

Super Cruise also compares GPS position with its map database. GM service information identifies the K179 Automated Driving Mapping Module and a LiDAR-scanned map database. Map and GPS-enhancement updates are downloaded through the vehicle’s OnStar Wi-Fi connection. The K73 telematics module supplies GPS and connectivity functions. If the vehicle cannot establish its location or does not have usable road data, Super Cruise cannot confirm that the road is eligible.

Before condemning hardware, verify the enabling conditions. Adaptive Cruise Control must be on, the Forward Collision System set to Alert and Brake, the road approved in the map database, lane markings visible, sensors unobstructed and the driver attentive. Teen Driver mode cannot be active. An OnStar plan and accepted terms may also be required. Requirements vary by model year and RPO, so identify the vehicle configuration before testing.

The secondary DIC message is often more useful than the general statement that Super Cruise is unavailable. “No Road Information” may indicate an ineligible road, an interchange, reconstruction, missing map data or lost GPS. The message “Sensors Can’t Find Lane Lines” can result from weak markings, glare or precipitation. “Sensor Blocked” points toward contamination. Other normal inhibits include an exit lane, a sharp curve, failure to center the vehicle or excessive speed. The referenced GM application lists 85 MPH, although limits are calibration-dependent.

“Could Not Recognize Face,” “Can’t See Face Clearly,” “Driver Attention Assist Unavailable,” momentary engagement followed by a takeover warning, and unexplained disengagement can originate in the monitoring system. Check for glare, a dirty lens, obstructions, steering-column position, a hand covering the infrared emitters, a loose B292 camera in the upper shroud, wiring damage or failed emitters. These complaints may occur without a DTC.

First, record the exact messages the customer received, along with road and location, weather, lighting, speed, engagement time and repeatability. Ask them about recent windshield, collision, steering, alignment, suspension, camera, radar or module work. Verify the OnStar account and terms when applicable, plus Wi-Fi and map-update status.

Next, perform GM’s vehicle diagnostic system check. Confirm battery state of charge, 9-16 V operating voltage where specified, clean and tight cables and grounds, intact fuses, seated connectors, correct power modes and the absence of interfering aftermarket equipment. Inspect lenses, radar areas and the steering-column camera before connecting the scan tool.

Run a full vehicle DTC scan and document every non-communicating module, DTC, symptom byte and current or history status. Do not erase evidence first. Diagnose voltage, internal-module, communication, power-mode and serial-data authentication faults before the Super Cruise symptom. Check applicable bulletins and calibrations. On covered 2021-2024 vehicles, intermittent startup U1624 in K124 may be a false loss-of-Ethernet fault caused by K73 telematics software; follow the bulletin and update K73. For other programmable modules, GM directs current software and a retest before replacement. Cruise data can retain the last eight disengagement reasons and the most recent engagement inhibit.

For “No Road Information” without a related DTC, move the vehicle to an open-sky area and inspect the K73 telematics data, including Number of Satellites Tracked when available. A value that remains at zero, or an incorrect location during an OnStar blue-button check, supports a GPS or telematics fault on vehicles covered by the applicable bulletin. Separate that failure from temporary map, road or reception limits.

For low-light face-recognition complaints, verify all three infrared emitters on each side of the steering-wheel light bar. GDS2 can command them through K124 Image Processing Module 1 Processor 2 under Configuration Reset Functions and Driver Monitoring System Illumination Command. GM recommends a phone camera with a long-exposure function because infrared output may be difficult to see. If one side is dark, follow the VIN-specific circuit diagnostics.

Programming, setup and calibration requirements differ across the 2019-2025 range. Confirm RPO content and follow the exact SI procedure after related components are replaced or disturbed. Some 2022-2023 vehicles with RPO 07Z use an image-processing module only to complete CAN circuits. Installing a functional replacement can create a “Take Steering Wheel” message unless the published configuration procedure is followed.

Complete all required programming, setup and calibrations, then clear the codes only as directed. Road-test the vehicle safely on a known compatible route and reproduce the original conditions. Confirm that the enabling indicators appear, the original DIC message does not return, driver monitoring responds and no faults reset. A successful bay check does not prove the complaint is resolved by itself.

“I’m a guy that started from ground zero. I mean, even though dad was running the place, I came in just like any other grunt, and I was expected to work, like any other grunt,” explains Loveland’s A-OK Transmission shop owner John Haines. “And my son is the same way. He’s starting at the bottom, working his way up.”

John’s son, Macen, represents the third generation of his family involved in the shop. But Loveland’s history goes back still further. This business has been in Springfield, Missouri, for more than 50 years.

“It was started by Don Loveland who retired in the mid-’70s when he sold the business to Amos Alsup, but retained ownership of the building,” John explains. “Dad [Vern Haines] came in in 1989. He started running the business side of things, taking over ownership in 2004. Then, I ran the day-to-day business for the last eight to ten years and took over the ownership role in January of 2025.”

John says some of their favorite work is on classic vehicles that owners entrust to his shop. “We’d had a little bit of a following with some of the car clubs, and I guess word of mouth just kind of took off from there. We do a lot of work for VL Classics in nearby Strafford, Missouri. And of course, anytime they sell a car, if it’s local, they recommend that those customers come here, and we’ve had the opportunity to work on a lot of those cars.

“These classic cars are their owners’ babies. They want to make sure they’re treated like their baby, and we make sure that everything is righteous with them. We cover the fenders and the doors anytime we’re doing any repair to keep anything from getting scratched or marked up. We do everything we can to keep them protected. When they get returned, they’re as clean or cleaner as when they got here.”

Beyond the classics, Loveland’s is a busy repair shop. “I enjoy the work,” John says. “I would say we just don’t have a typical customer. We’ve got everybody from schoolteachers and soccer moms to a plumber who’s trying to make a living using their van or truck to get to the next jobsite. Many customers are that blue collar crowd, people who have to make a living too.

“We’ve garnered a reputation of being fair on price. I’m not going be the cheapest guy in town by any means, and I’m going to try not to be the most expensive. I’m making sure my work is comparable for the price I’m asking.”
He achieves this in part by taking another step beyond the initial repair.

“Anytime we have a customer that has a repair, especially a transmission repair, I remind them that after 500-600 miles, I want to see the car back. They don’t have to have an appointment. It doesn’t cost them anything. I just want to check everything over. That tells the customer, we’re not here just to take their money. We want to make sure that the job’s good when they’ve driven a few hundred miles. If there’s a problem, it usually will show up then. It just gives that perceived notion of, ‘well, hey, they’re not just here to take my money and run.’

“Another thing I do is remind them about service intervals. Let’s face it, the biggest reason why a lot of transmissions fail nowadays is because somebody bought into the myth of you don’t ever have to change the transmission fluid. That’s not the case! A lot of times I’ll tell the customer I’d like to see it back for a fluid change at 25,000 miles just to keep that relationship going because most customers, if they’ve put a transmission in a car, are going to come back to the same shop, especially if it’s going to be for maintenance work on that transmission.

“I’ve done more R&R work as of lately. It’s been a cost-to-benefit analysis thing. Like if someone wants a 700 R4 in a classic Camaro or something like that, I’ll build it for them. TH350s and 400s or C4s and C6s are units that you can’t really get reman anymore. A lot of the later model stuff, the six-, eight- or 10-speeds, we get from reman. By the time I buy the parts and spend the time and labor to build it, I’m money ahead to buy the reman and just put it in. At the end of the day, I come out a little cheaper on the on the build side, plus if something goes wrong with that unit, I’m being paid to fix it.”

“As for the CVTs, I don’t build those at all. Mainly, I just don’t have the space to keep all the stuff I need to build them properly. I’d go reman on them anytime I can. About the only CVT that I ever put in as a used unit would be a Subaru. I don’t know why, but they just seem to work.”

Haines goes on to say that about half the jobs going through his bays are general repair work. “I let customers know that we do more than transmissions,” he elaborates. “If your car needs a tune-up, if you just need a headlight put in, we’ll take care of it. We’ll make sure you’re good and going down the road.”

Finally, John recognizes that training for the six-member staff at the shop is important. He says the shop pays for the classes, room and board for seminars that are within a day’s drive. He adds that anytime one of the local parts houses puts on a training class, the Loveland’s team will be there.
Your class has been assigned an innovation project.

Nobody has to invent a new vehicle, build a robot or promise to revolutionize transportation by Friday. The challenge is closer to home: improve one routine that makes your school’s shop harder to use.

The idea follows a point Jeremy White made during his keynote at the 2026 Schaeffler Automotive Symposium. The WIRED Senior Innovation Editor argued that the most interesting uses of technology come from reconsidering how work is organized, rather than simply fitting a new tool into an existing routine.

Students can test that thinking on something they understand. Tool checkout, parts requests, inspection documentation or project handoffs could all provide manageable subjects. Instructors should select processes students are authorized to examine and keep safety procedures outside the scope of unsupervised changes.

Begin with observation. Have teams watch how the current process works and talk with the people using it. Where does someone wait? What information is frequently missing? Which step causes confusion? Require a specific problem statement before students propose a solution.

Next, establish a starting measurement. A team examining tool checkout might record how long the process takes or how often a tool’s location is unknown. Students should collect only appropriate information and avoid identifying classmates unnecessarily.

Then design a small improvement. Computing might help through a simple form, shared inventory record or spreadsheet. Students could also discover that clearer instructions or a better physical arrangement solves much of the problem. Their job is to justify the choice, including who will maintain it.

An instructor-approved trial provides the next lesson. Does the proposal work when people are busy? Can a new user understand it? What happens when someone enters incomplete information? Teams should document those exceptions and revise their approach.
Finish with a presentation comparing the result with the original measurement. An unsuccessful trial can still earn a strong evaluation if students explain the evidence and what they would change.
This project brings together communication, observation and practical use of information. It also introduces a business reality: an improvement has to work for the people expected to use it.
This concept invites industries to rethink familiar practices. Your classroom can begin with a process small enough to change and important enough that somebody notices when it gets better.
And we’d love to hear about it! Share your ideas with me at [email protected]. I’d love to share them with the rest of the Tomorrow’s Technician audience.
China has proposed a new draft rule to set standards for remanufactured auto parts, according to multiple media sources.
Business Today Malaysia reports the proposal sets requirements for sourcing used components, product quality, traceability, and market supervision.
The draft rules focus on collecting, processing, labeling, and selling parts recovered from end-of-life vehicles, according to the article.
“They aim to ensure remanufactured components meet or exceed the quality of equivalent new products,” the article states.
Bloomberg reports that the proposal would provide product traceability and more oversight of the remanufacturing market.
Engines, steering systems, transmissions, front and rear axles, and vehicle frames are all parts that could be regulated, Business Today adds.

“Remanufacturers would be required to obtain these components through qualified vehicle dismantlers and ensure the recovered parts correspond to the products they intend to remanufacture,” Business Today states.
The proposal would prohibit the remanufacturing of exhaust after-treatment devices.

Automotive parts costs began increasing around the summer of 2025, according to Ryan Mandell of Mitchell. Mandell said the company has observed higher average parts prices as U.S. tariff policy affects OEM costs.
Mitchell saw parts inflation accelerate during the second half of 2025. Mandell said the company expects additional price increases as OEMs respond to tariff-related expenses.
Automotive Parts Costs Could Rise Further
Mandell also pointed to reshoring as another factor that could affect pricing.

As OEMs move more manufacturing operations back to the U.S., they can avoid tariffs on some imported parts. However, Mandell said domestic manufacturing generally carries higher labor costs than overseas production.
Those higher labor costs could contribute to another round of parts price increases as more production returns to the U.S.
